text: Is the 21st century defined by genres that never go mainstream but impact pop music anyway? My daughter was listening to "Say So" by Doja Cat on YouTube. And I asked her to replay it because something sounded eerily familiar—as if I heard it before. Turns out, it sounds remarkably similar to the future funk song "Fiona Coyne" by Skylar Spence. If you're unaware, future funk is a genre that originated in the 2010s. It's basically a mix of disco and vaporwave. It has its following, but never cracked the mainstream. But hold on... "Fiona Coyne" is inspired by "Love Talkin' (Honey It's You)" by Tatsuro Yamashita, one of the heavyweights of city pop. City pop is what's known as a retronym. That is, a label we give to music when a retrospective canon gets formed, requiring recontextualization. Yacht rock is another example of a retronym. In Japan, where city pop originates from, city pop is an obscure genre even though city pop songs themselves are popular. That's because it was simply mainstream pop in Japan. Now don't get me wrong. "City pop" as a term existed in Japan during the 80s. But this wasn't a genre with a defined musical structure. It was more a marketing term to sell aspiration, much like how we in the West hear terms like "contemporary" and "sophisti-pop". Because of this, most Japanese people didn't recognize city pop as an identifiable thing . Fast forward to the 21st century. Westerners started hearing Japanese music from the 80s. They needed context. So they re-purposed a Japanese marketing term to define a corpus, a body of work that identified Japanese music with broad similarities that seemed to have an associated scene. The city pop canon was never big in the West. Even now, it's only known amongst music nerds. But its effect on modern mainstream music is huge . Here's examples: - "Out of Time" by The Weeknd samples Tomoko Aran's "Midnight Pretenders" - "GONE, GONE / THANK YOU" by Tyler, the Creator interpolates Tatsuro Yamashita's "Fragile" - "We Ride" by Brave Girls was a Top 5 K-pop hit, but it was blatantly marketed as city pop upon its release What's wild? City pop is not the only obscure genre to impact the mainstream but never hit the mainstream. Witch house, phonk, and vaporwave all had a big impact. But none of the artists who originated these genres have ever become house house names. I think this is one of the defining characteristics of 21st-century music. A genre can remain underground while its sounds, production techniques, and aesthetics become completely mainstream. We're in a time where the mainstream raids from subculture before subculture can ever challenge it. Is this why we no longer see musical revolutions like jazz, rock, punk, hip hop, and grunge? Has the mainstream become so good at absorbing underground music that new genres can influence it without ever displacing or fundamentally transforming it?
label: Deep Analysis

text: The long instrumental outro on “People Make the World Go Round” might be the real heart of the song The long version of “People Make the World Go Round” has a whole second half, and I think it’s the best part https://youtu.be/2owZXPyeilc?si=pq2Q5CoSjFxLEqN- Most people probably know “People Make the World Go Round” from the single, which is around 3:30. That version is already great. Thom Bell’s arrangement, Linda Creed’s lyrics, Russell Thompkins Jr. singing in that ridiculous falsetto. But the album version on The Stylistics’ first record is over six minutes long, and right around the point where the single fades out, it just keeps going. And honestly, that’s the part I like the most. The vocals slowly disappear and the whole thing opens up. Bass, drums, congas, all those strange Bell percussion sounds, then guitar and flute drifting in and out. It doesn’t really feel like it’s trying to get anywhere anymore. It just sits in the groove. That part hits me more physically than the first half. It’s hard to explain without sounding slightly ridiculous, but it feels like the song starts breathing differently. The lyrics are actually pretty bleak. Strikes, garbage piling up, pollution, Wall Street losing money. The whole world is dysfunctional. Then the words disappear and the music just keeps going. To me it almost feels like the song is saying: yeah, the world is a mess, but it keeps turning anyway. That’s obviously just my interpretation, but once I started hearing it like that I couldn’t really unhear it. I also found something interesting about the rhythm. I assumed the long instrumental part felt more relaxed because it probably settled into a simple 4/4 groove. Apparently not. The ending vamp has been analysed as alternating between 4/4 and 5/4. Which is kind of funny, because it feels more relaxed even though the meter is actually less regular. Maybe that extra beat is part of why it feels so loose, like the music is constantly hanging around a little longer than you expect. The song also seems to have really appealed to jazz and soul-jazz musicians. Milt Jackson did an eight-minute version, Cleveland Eaton covered it, O’Donel Levy did a great guitar version, and it kept resurfacing later in hip hop and sample culture. I don’t want to claim all those musicians were specifically obsessed with the long Stylistics outro, because there’s no way to know that. But it does feel like there was something in the composition that musicians wanted to stretch out and live inside. Does the long outro change the meaning of the song for you, or does it just feel like an extended groove? And for anyone here who understands the meter better than I do, why does that 4/4 and 5/4 vamp feel so relaxed when the rhythm is actually becoming less regular? If you only know the short version, let the album version keep running past the point where the single would have faded out. That’s where the song really starts for me.
label: Deep Analysis

text: How much can an album’s last track change the meaning of everything before it? I've been thinking about how much weight the final track of an album can carry. Sometimes an album seems to be telling you one story, but the ending makes you reconsider everything that came before it. A tragic ending can make earlier moments of confidence feel more like denial. A hopeful ending can make everything that seemed hopeless before it feel completely different. But I think there's a fine line between an ending that genuinely changes your perspective and one that feels forced. If the rest of the album hasn't earned that conclusion, even a beautiful final track might not be enough to make it convincing. And I'm not necessarily talking about albums where the closing track is the best song. I'm more interested in endings that change how you interpret the earlier tracks when you listen again. Have you ever experienced that with an album? What was it, and what specifically changed about how you heard the rest of it after reaching the end?
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: Would a Supergroup of Established Solo Artists Work Musically? What if some of the biggest male artists across different generations and genres came together to form a boy band? Imagine a supergroup featuring Jungkook, Bruno Mars, Justin Bieber, and The Kid LAROI, with potential additions like The Weeknd, Chris Brown, or even Kendrick Lamar as the main rapper. The idea would be to combine artists whose talents transcend different eras of music. Between their vocals, songwriting, dancing, stage presence, and musical versatility, this group could potentially create something incredible. The biggest challenge would probably be distributing lines and balancing so many talented singers. Some additional role diversity might help, but each artist already brings something different to the table. Jungkook — The All-Rounder Jungkook brings powerful vocals, impressive dancing, and years of experience performing in BTS. His experience working within a group would be especially valuable when it comes to choreography, teamwork, and balancing individual performances. He could help bring everyone together. Bruno Mars — The Veteran Performer Bruno brings incredible versatility, experience, and stage presence. His ability to move between pop, funk, R&B, and soul would give the group plenty of musical flexibility. He's also an excellent live performer and songwriter who could contribute to the group's longevity. Justin Bieber — The Pop and R&B Specialist Bieber has an impressive track record spanning multiple eras of pop music. Beyond his recognizable voice and massive popularity, he brings songwriting experience, musical instincts, and an understanding of how to create successful records. His versatility would make him another valuable member. The Kid LAROI — The Younger Perspective LAROI brings a different energy through his blend of melodic rap, pop, and R&B. His ability to experiment with different sounds could help the group explore multiple musical directions. His emotional delivery and distinctive vocal style would complement the other members. While he might not be as dance-oriented as Jungkook or Bruno, his strengths as a vocalist and songwriter could make him an important part of the lineup. Kendrick Lamar — The Main Rapper Kendrick would bring a strong rap presence to every track, adding another dimension to the group's sound. His incredible lyricism, storytelling, flow, and songwriting abilities would make him an essential member of the lineup. His versatility would allow him to complement the group's pop and R&B influences while bringing his own unique style. He could also work alongside The Kid LAROI on rap sections, giving the group even more musical flexibility. The Weeknd or Chris Brown — Alternative Additions Both could fit into the lineup for different reasons. The Weeknd would bring his distinctive vocals, atmospheric R&B sound, and ability to create memorable melodies. Chris Brown would contribute strong R&B vocals, dancing, and performance experience, adding another member capable of handling demanding choreography. The Big Question Would a supergroup with this much individual talent actually work? With so many established solo artists, balancing creative control, musical direction, and line distribution could be difficult. However, their different strengths could also lead to some incredible collaborations. Who would make your ideal lineup? Would you keep these artists, replace anyone, or add someone who brings a completely different skill set? And most importantly, what kind of music should a group like this make?
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: The Disconnect Between Favorite Songs Of The 90s & Hit Singles Of The 90s The American radio station KEXP recently aired a countdown of KEXP Listeners’ Favorite Songs Of The 90s. It’s a good list to check out. However, the thing that struck me immediately is how some of these songs weren’t hits in their time - they were either slow burns that have accumulated fans over time or have been used in media after their release and have become notable. Here are the top 10 songs on the list [spoiler] followed by their chart performance in the US and UK. Beck “Loser” (US #10 / UK #15) Soundgarden “Black Hole Sun” (US - / UK #12) Radiohead “Creep” (US #34 / UK #7) Deee-Lite “Groove Is In The Heart” (US #4 / UK #2) Massive Attack “Teardrop” (US - / UK #10) Radiohead “Paranoid Android” (US - / UK #3) The Breeders “Cannonball” (US #44 / UK #40) Beastie Boys “Sabotage” (US - / UK #19) Mazzy Star “Fade Into You” (US #44 / UK #48) Nirvana “Smells Like Teen Spirit” (US #6 / UK #7) I’m not arguing against any of these picks, they are all great songs. What is fascinating to me how far away from hits that some of these songs were - “Cannonball” and “Fade Into You” in particular were not notable as singles but have grown in time to iconic 90s songs. Just for fun, the year 1994 is overrepresented in the top 10 above: four of the ten songs were released as singles in 1994. What were the top singles in the US and UK in 1994? “The Sign” by Ace Of Base and “Love Is All Around” by Wet Wet Wet. It’s worth noting: the listenership of KEXP skews older and more towards rock. That said, ask the same question on this sub and you might arrive at a similar answer. I’m interested to hear what people think about how favorite songs 30 years on differs so greatly from what was popular in its time. If you ask about favorites songs of the 90s in 20 years, will the answers change again?
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: Where have all the epic melodies gone? I’m a 90’s/2000’s kid, so not like I’ve any inherent bias for the stuff I’m talking about, which seemed to abound more from the 50’s to 70’s & 80’s. It’s just that I’ve noticed a distinct lack of these epic, memorable, melodies like you often heard in tracks back then, and I’m wondering why that might be. I’m a musician myself and am well aware most all songs will have some kind of melody, thanks, but, again, I’m talking the truly epic global smash hit melodies anyone would know- things which effectively have become standards… stuff like Happy Together, Sound of Silence, Strangers in The Night, and of course countless others. The melodies are so strong they’re almost palpable. But with every passing decade, the emphasis on and desire for such strong melodies seems to fade. For as many smash hit songs as came out in the 80’s, already these style melodies seemed to be on a decline by then. Again, everything has melody, much of it can be catchy, but not necessarily epic. I’d also love to know some contemporary tracks/artists you might recommend who you feel feature such big melodies. From what I’ve heard, Father John Misty seems to like to do this kind of thing, though I might be conflating use of string sections and a general 70’s sound with epic melody. In fact, there are none melodies more epic than the ones you’d find in classical music, but I guess I wanted to focus more on “pop” or whatever cats like Humperdinck, Jones, Elvis, Vinton, ABBA, Simon & Garfunkel, etc etc were doing is called.

text: What makes you follow-up with or ignore a music recommendation from someone else? Doesn't necessarily have to be a person, it could also be like a streaming/YouTube recommendation. For example, I noticed for me I usually don't follow-up on a recommendation when I know that person has a massively different music taste that my taste doesn't really align with or when they've consistently recommended music I don't have a taste for, even when they show me some songs that I kind of do like in the moment, but wouldn't necessarily listen to on my own. It's kind of intriguing though because in the dozens of songs they've shared with me, 2-3 of them I've actually really come to enjoy and saved, but it's rare given our very different music tastes, so I generally find myself not fully engaged when they recommend me music or deeply go into the context of it. And then for someone else who's music taste does intersect with mine, I find myself following-up more with their song recommendations and more frequently finding songs from them I enjoy. As for digital recommendations, it usually has to hook me quickly in the beginning with instrumentals I enjoy/be a song from someone I'm familiar with, or I'll just skip and don't end up giving the rest of the song a try.

text: So, what's the deal with "Portugal. The Man?" Besides the Punctuation? So this is a band I was introduced to at Lollapalooza back in 2018, and they really hit a chord -- they had this really cool progressive streak, impeccable playing, very tight rhythms, and sorta 70s style falsetto funky smoothness. And weird (e.g. "[AKA M80 the Wolf](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8YRccJrn4M0)"). I was instantly attracted. At times the guitar felt like he was channeling Carlos Santana at Woodstock, other times Barry Gibb. They were pretty unknown at the time - the Album was The Satanic Satanist - tongue-in-cheek but also serious ("[People Say](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhAQYwxifS0)" was the 'hit'). It was considered their breakthrough album at that time as their earlier stuff was even stranger. I listened to a lot of that album and went to their back catalog, and saw them several times. All that, and I will honestly say they are a band that is easy to like but hard to love. There's a distant coldness about them, probably driven by John Gourley's introversion and perhaps a feeling of not being totally let into their world. It's more like "see what we can do" rather than "here is who we are." Oh, yeah, and the band's name is kinda annoying -- who puts punctuation into their name for gawd's sake? ;) I read they did it because they were trying to evoke a character named "Portugal." Fast forward to today, and most people know "[Feel It Still](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZSF4LJLYByU)" as the big hit but don't really know the band. I feel like either the band really wants to remain underground, or wants to break through but doesn't quite know how. I have most of their albums (haven't picked up Shish yet), most of them have good to great reviews, and I do listen regularly but don't enjoy them as much as that first album. Even so, I am always impressed by their songwriting and their alt-progressive-rock chops. Is that their destiny until they find some other way? Just be happy with what they do? text: Do 'deep cuts' actually make an album better? I've been thinking a lot lately about albums that are praised for their 'deep cuts' - those tracks that aren't singles but are supposedly essential to the album's overall quality or artistic statement. On one hand, I get it. Sometimes, those less-played tracks reveal a different side of the artist, showcase experimental ideas, or provide crucial thematic depth that the singles can't. They can make an album feel more substantial and rewarding on repeated listens. But then, I also wonder if sometimes this praise for deep cuts is a bit of a music fan's intellectualization. Is there a point where an album has too many 'deep cuts' and not enough genuinely strong, memorable songs? Does the presence of a few standout non-singles automatically elevate an album that might otherwise be just okay? Or are we sometimes just looking for reasons to appreciate every track, especially from artists we already admire? I've definitely found albums where the deep cuts became my absolute favorites, revealing layers I missed on first listen. But I've also listened to albums where the 'deep cuts' just felt like filler, and the album would have been stronger if it were shorter and more focused. What are your thoughts? Do deep cuts genuinely make an album better, or is it more about the overall consistency and quality of every track, regardless of its 'single' status?

text: Why do people like old-time mountain music better than bluegrass? I am firmly a bluegrass fan and have never been a huge fan of old-time to be honest. Bluegrass is just such an iconic genre, and you really can’t beat the drive and precision of Scruggs-style three-finger banjo picking. Yet nearly every time I talk to musicians who play both or lean heavily into traditional Appalachian roots, there seems to be an insistence that old-time is the deeper, more authentic, or outright "superior" tradition. From an outsider’s perspective, the musical priorities couldn't be more distinct. Bluegrass emerged as a modern, stage-focused art form. Bill Monroe, Earl Scruggs, and the Stanley Brothers took traditional string band elements and electrified them with jazz-like soloing, breakneck tempos, strict rhythmic chop chords, and soaring "high lonesome" vocal harmonies. It is fundamentally an ensemble performance built around individual virtuosity: each musician steps forward to take a blistering break on the banjo, fiddle, mandolin, or flatpicked acoustic guitar, trading leads while the rest of the rhythm section locks down a relentless drive. The technical ceiling is exceptionally high, and the tight arrangements reward intense instrumental discipline. Old-time, by contrast, operates on an entirely different philosophy centered on communal rhythm and dance. Instead of Scruggs-style syncopated rolls, old-time banjo relies on clawhammer and frailing techniques that meld percussive downstrokes directly with the melody. There are rarely individual solo breaks; instead, the fiddle and banjo lock into unison melodic lines while the guitar and bass anchor a hypnotic, circular groove meant to drive square dances and front-porch sessions for hours without stopping. Old-time advocates often praise this exact quality: the absence of competitive soloing creates an egalitarian space where players merge into a single texture rather than showing off technical gymnastics. The crooked tunes, modal tunings, and raw, unpolished tone carry a direct, haunting connection to pre-commercial Anglo-Celtic and African-American folk roots that bluegrass modernized and commercialized. While I can appreciate the historic weight and trance-like groove of old-time fiddling, the sheer energy, structural complexity, and vocal power of bluegrass always feel vastly more compelling to listen to. Old-time often feels like music that is significantly more fun to play in a jam circle than it is to sit and listen to as an audience member, whereas bluegrass commands the stage with dynamic range and jaw-dropping execution. For those who actively prefer old-time over bluegrass: what is the core aesthetic pull that makes it superior to you? Is it the communal dance groove, the historical grit, or simply an aversion to the rigid, polished showmanship that defines modern bluegrass?
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: I want to give a shout out to Swans’s gothic era! Took some time to go back to a couple of Swans albums. Revisited Children of God, White Light from the Mouth of Infinity & The Great Annihilator. Then I went back to Love of Life & The Burning World. And I have to say, this part of their career is very very interesting! I mean, what they pulled off on those albums is astounding when you consider the existence of Filth & Cop. Those two albums are like trying to dominate someone & succeeding….in the most brutal fashion that you could think of. Uncompromising, harsh, scary, full of rage & hate. The most pessimistic view of humanity that you could get. Reminded me of an extremely violent section of a bar that’s full of “FUCK YOU” graffiti. Someone shaking their fist at you & pounding you into submission until there’s blood left over. But My God….what Swans transformed into from Children of God to The Great Annihilator is unbelievable! There’s a constant mixture of darkness & beauty that’s really fascinating. Lush textures, ethereal keyboards, guitars that are elegant or luscious instead of “rip your face off”. So many lovely melodies. But there’s always an unsettling vibe. Embracing the macabre or disturbing parts of life. Haunting and luxurious at the same time. And I love the gothic/folky bits. Crazy how they pulled them off so well considering their No Wave/noise rock roots. Adding acoustic guitars into the mix, softening their style & going for “existential” rather than “violent”…..so awesome to me. Sorrowful but really captivating. There’s something about this era that reminded me of groups like the Velvet Underground, Joy Division & Leonard Cohen. Or even Wire/Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds. Great storytelling. Like you’re huddled around a bunch of people in a room, sharing their experiences late at night with the moon shingling through the window. I could totally include tracks from Children of God to The Great Annihilator in a playlist that has Bauhaus, the Cure, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Echo & the Bunnymen, etc. I really appreciate Jarboe’s contributions too! Hearing her vocals, seeing her songwriting credits & knowing that she played keyboard parts….I really like that. Gave a nice contrast to Michael Gira, added some variety. I think that Jarboe really emphasized that “darkness + beauty” thing that I mentioned earlier. Along with showing how much Swans changed from Filth & Cop. I like Soundtracks for the Blind & a lot of the post-reunion stuff too. But I think that the run from Children of God to The Great Annihilator deserves some love. Demonstrates that Swans is more than a crazy noise band haha!
label: Deep Analysis

text: What actually makes something “metal”? How would you turn something completely unorthodox into metal? I'm not asking which bands or songs count as metal. I'm more interested in what the actual musical ingredients of “metalness” are. For example, suppose you were given something that has absolutely nothing to do with metal — a barbershop quartet, a recorder/flute melody, a children's song, an old folk tune, etc. What would you actually have to change or add to make it sound convincingly metal? Are there specific parameters that tend to matter, such as: Rhythm/groove and how the notes are accented Tempo or time signatures Types of chord progressions or intervals Melody and harmony Dissonance Instrumentation and tone Distortion, amplification, or production Certain approaches to riffs Drum patterns Dynamics and articulation Basically, I'm wondering if there are underlying musical characteristics that can be applied to almost any source material and make it sound metal. For example, if I took a barbershop quartet arrangement and kept the basic melodies/harmonies intact, what would I need to do to it for someone to hear it and immediately think, “that's metal”? And what about something even stranger, like taking a melody written for a recorder and trying to make the recorder itself sound metal? I'm looking for more of a music-theory/compositional explanation than a list of genre conventions. Is there a sort of “recipe” for making something metal, even if the original material is completely un-metal?
label: Deep Analysis

text: The debate between band performing live and using backing tracks I just listened to an interesting interview with Fil Henley who has a YouTube channel "Wings of Pegasus" where he analyzes and points out bands that use pre-recorded tracks while performing in concert. This sort of audio enhancement has been going on for decades, especially in concert albums. Then came Milli Vanilli, then came Ashlee Simpson, etc, etc. You have one side that say that for the money being spent, the music should be live, at least most of it anyways. Some instruments/vocals are hard to recreate live, so you slip it in here in there. The issue comes when most of what you're seeing is being "mimed" (as Fil Henley likes to say) Then there are the accusations of fakery, misdirection, being duped, etc. Music should be organic, faults and all. Then you have the other side who say, well, who cares? They're representing the spirit of the music, I'm seeing my favorite band/artist and that's what really counts. Music is a subjective experience. As for the promoters? Hell, they don't care as long as tickets are being sold. Perhaps it's just a product of the times, it's inevitable with advances in technology that this was going to happen. There were 2 points in the interview that stood out. One, it's the fact that people are accepting this that made the interviewer (who will remain nameless because of how polarizing he is) go ballistic. What happened to the genuine live experience? Secondly, maybe there should be some "labelling" of concerts so people know what they're going into (sort of like "organic" labels) that there will be backing tracks, vocals will be mimed, etc. Fil Henley is an interesting case, because as a former musician and audio engineer, he's merely pointing out the truth. Bryan Adams filed a complaint with YouTube about him, and YouTube sided with Henley, that hey, he's just pointing out facts! Not sure where this going, I'm pretty sure this is a product of the times/technology, but it definitely makes for some food for thought. Will people care? Probably not. What's around the corner? Who knows. Do we ever see what's coming? Never.

text: "Everything I believe in is telling me that I want more, more, more": a defense for Oasis's post-90s discography There seems to be an unspoken rule that every musician has their "expiration date". After they've produced the work that's responsible for their role within pop culture and the zeitgeist, everything afterwards feels superfluous, almost pointless. The only people who seemingly enjoy it are the hardcore fans. Dig Out Your Soul, Oasis's last album, turns 18 today. It's easily one of my favorites by them. I think it helped that I explored it before I was aware of the whole "they peaked in the 90s" notion. The first six tracks remain one of the best runs in their discography: the rise and fall of "The Turning", the Doors-inspired swagger of "Waiting for the Rapture", and the true final hurrah for the band, the euphoric head rush that's "The Shock of the Lightning" (a drum solo on an Oasis track?? Who knew!) The album loses it's focus towards the end, but there's still the likes of "Falling Down" and "Soldier On" that help make the bumpier back half at least memorable. It's an album that has more to offer than it's reputation (or lack thereof), particularly for people who check out of the band after their first two albums... ....and yet when I got into their 90s output two years later, I inexplicably fell down the same path. I too fell hook, line and sinker for the narrative about everything after What's the Story Morning Glory being slim pickings. "Beware all ye who go past Be Here Now. Do not go past jail." It wasn't until I was in college that I just got so into them that I thought, "Fuck it" and checked out...and was pleasantly surprised. While they never made an album as consistent as those first two (and who can?), there's plenty of amazing songs that feel necessary to be included in their "canon" (i.e. the type of tracks that would be glaring omissions from a Greatest Hits compilation). I don't think it's even a hot take to consider some of these tracks from this stretch to be just as good as those from their golden period. Even the B-sides, an ace in the hole that Oasis were known for, were still otherworldly. For example, I'd consider "Let's All Make Believe", the B-side to "Go Let it Out", to be one of the best songs Noel's ever written... Strangle my hope and make me pray, to a God I've never seen but who I betray. It's an incredibly vulnerable snapshot of Oasis MK 1 (i.e. the brothers Gallagher and Alan White with Guigsy and Bonehead) falling apart. It's one of the most cathartic and honest songs in their discography...and they stuck the mother on a B-side! Standing on the Shoulders of Giants, the album whose sessions produced that song, is an interesting turning point for the band, fittingly the start to their Y2K run. It's kind of like Blur's self-titled album, with the band being at a stylistic and emotional crossroads: Noel bought a bunch of pedals and was curious about new sonic possibilities and contemporary influences, all while kicking drugs, realizing that the band was shedding two of its oldest members, and recognizing that the Britpop bubble was bursting. It's an incredible snapshot of post-party depression: poignant numbers like "Where did it All Go Wrong?", "Sunday Morning Call", and the beloved fan favorite "Gas Panic!"... That my family don’t seem so familiar And my enemies all know my name And if you hear me tap on your window Better get on yer knees and pray panic is on the way ...not to mention the terrific b-sides, like the aforementioned "Let's All Make Believe" and lethargically hungover tracks like "Cigarettes in Hell" and "One Way Road". The whole effect is a very sobering one, a sharp contrast from the happy-go-lucky effortless confidence of "Live Forever" and "Some Might Say". It's not all doom and gloom though: "Go Let it Out", the lead single, feels like a total rebirth for the band. The 60's psychedelic mellotron paired with the triphop drumbeat feels like this perfect new strand, something very retro, but very Y2K as well. I can picture someone listening to them back in the day thinking, "Hallelujah!" I'd still put it (i.e., the A-side and it's two B-sides) up there with any of their best in their entire run. Heathen Chemistry and Don't Believe the Truth, the two albums that followed, are more mixed bags. The former especially, a transitional record as the band was starting from scratch with new members Gem Archer and Andy Bell, is easily my pick for their worst album period. But a number of songs on there are still all-timers for me. There's the high and mighty lead single, "Hindu Times", but the fan favorite became "Little by Little", a song that became such a barnburner during its time that the brothers brought it back for their reunion tour last year. More interestingly though, it's the album where Liam started coming into his own as a writer too. There's the lovely Rubber Soul-coded "Songbird", a song with an almost uncharacteristic innocence to it ("She's a little pilot in my mind"), and the surprisingly cathartic "Born on a Different Cloud". Don't Believe the Truth, more of a move in the right direction, started really producing the crown jewels. No Oasis career retrospective would be complete without "Lyla" and "The Importance of Being Idle", further proof that Noel hadn't lost his penchant for writing anthems. Liam brings an interesting yin and yang with his co-writes with Gem Archer: the wonderful ruckus of "Meaning of Soul" (speed-induced skiffle...also clock that harmonica solo!) and the wonderfully titled "Guess God Thinks I'm Abel". The brothers share vocals, a rarity, on perhaps the best closer in their 2000's albums: "Let There Be Love". And again, I'd be remiss not to mention those b-sides . How the Neil Young-inspired "Shout it Out Loud" didn't make the cut is beyond me. I've been giving Gem and Andy the cold shoulder, but the latter's "Thank You for the Good Times" has a great victory lap feel to it. One could almost picture it as a triumphant album closer. Starting with Be Here Now, you get some sense that the tracks that were placed as extras on singles were the stylistic curveballs, showing a side of the band that would surprise most. Nowhere is this more apparent than the elusive "Idler's Dream". It's perhaps the most un-Oasisy track they ever did: just Noel and a piano. And it yet it works so well! I think a lot of people see Oasis's later albums like, say, the most recent few seasons of The Simpsons: a shadow of their 90s glory days and the kind of highs that most creatives strive to reach. But I'd compare it more to the last two seasons of Community. Saying that any of those later ones are better would be somewhat of an unpopular opinion, and it's not all amazing, but they're still quite good. And the episodes that do hit, hit just as hard as the cream from the prior crop...if not more so. Up until a few years ago, I saw a band's discography as "The albums that build up to the masterpiece, the masterpiece, and chasing the masterpiece." "Why are U2 still making albums that nobody cares about?" What an arrogant, naive thing to say. I don't know if it comes from reading more about artists or being more involved in the process myself, but I've learned to take artists on their own terms and to not go in with expectations. You might be surprised. I've talked at length about how fascinating the Beach Boys post- Pet Sounds discography, a run of stuff that I stupidly chalked up to "licking their wounds after Smile and hunting for another Pet Sounds ." And sure, some artists do this. But for the most part, it's just people making stuff that they want to make, the way they've always worked. And I think Oasis are a great example of this, whether it's stylistic anomalies like Standing on the Shoulders of Giants, the crowd-pleasing stompers, that continued to win fans over, or the B-side tracks that feel like the audible equivalent of buried treasure. If anyone is in love with their 90's stuff and is contemplating taking the plunge, please do! It's well worth your time :)

text: How much should an artist’s intended meaning matter to a listener’s interpretation? I’ve been thinking about the relationship between what an artist intends a song to mean and what a listener personally takes from it. What prompted this was properly listening to Chappell Roan ’s Good Luck, Babe! for the first time a few days ago. I’d heard parts of the song in passing on Instagram Reels before, but I had never actually sat down and listened to the whole thing. Since then, I genuinely haven’t been able to get it out of my head. I’m a straight guy, and I absolutely love the song. Musically and emotionally, everything about it works for me, but I’m especially obsessed with the outro and the way the song gradually winds down. There’s something about that ending that hits me every single time. Because I became slightly obsessed with it, I started reading Reddit threads, Twitter posts, Instagram comments, and other discussions to see how people reacted to the song and interpreted it. Most of the discussion understandably revolves around queer identity, repression, compulsory heterosexuality, and someone trying to deny or suppress their sexuality. That is how I understand the song’s central narrative, too. That meaning was apparent to me when I first listened to it. I understood the narrator as addressing another woman, and I’m not suggesting that the song is secretly about something else or that its queer meaning should somehow be replaced by my interpretation. What I find interesting is that, emotionally, my brain takes the song somewhere completely different. For some reason, I strongly associate it with mental-health struggles and the experience of trying to suppress something inside yourself. The central idea of desperately trying to push away a feeling that keeps returning makes me think about knowing that something is wrong internally while continuing to behave as though everything is normal. Even the parts of the song about going out, being with other people, and trying to move forward register differently for me. I imagine someone throwing themselves into social situations, relationships, distractions, or whatever else they can find because they’re trying to convince themselves that they’re okay. From the outside, they might be socializing, meeting people and apparently living normally, while internally they know they’re struggling and aren’t really confronting it. That obviously isn’t the literal narrative of Good Luck, Babe! . But every time I listen to it, that is where my emotional interpretation goes. I understand what the song is describing, yet it has somehow attached itself to a completely different experience in my own head. And that made me wonder more broadly about how we interpret music. My tentative view is that a personal association can be meaningful without being a claim about what the lyrics literally describe. But I’m unsure whether ‘interpretation’ is the right word for that distinction. I also wonder where people draw the line between interpreting a work and simply projecting onto it . If the actual lyrics clearly describe one experience, but the emotions, imagery or general themes make a listener connect it to something else entirely, is that still an interpretation of the song? Or is the song simply becoming a vehicle for an experience the listener already carries with them? How much weight do you personally give to an artist’s intended meaning once a song becomes meaningful to you? Can a personal interpretation be completely legitimate even when it is quite far removed from the literal narrative of the lyrics? I’m particularly interested in songs where you understand the artist’s intended meaning, but the song has nevertheless come to represent something completely different in your own life. What in the music or lyrics creates that connection for you?

text: What actually makes a band sound like themselves, even when everything else changes? I've gone down a music rabbit hole the last couple days trying to figure out what actually makes a band recognizable as that band. I've been calling it a band's "fingerprint" because I don't really have a better word for it. Not necessarily their genre, a particular guitar tone, or even the singer's voice. Just whatever combination of things makes your brain recognize who's playing before you actually check. Breaking Benjamin is probably my best example because I've listened to basically their entire catalog. They've evolved, production has changed, and the lineup has changed dramatically, but there's still something that immediately sounds like Breaking Benjamin to me. Motionless in White's "Masterpiece" is actually what got me thinking about this from the opposite direction. When I first heard it, my brain basically went, "Wait... is this Breaking Benjamin? It sounds like Breaking Benjamin, but something is off." Obviously it wasn't them. But another band had apparently gotten close enough to whatever my brain associates with Breaking Benjamin that it triggered that recognition anyway. Then I had almost the opposite experience with Bullet For My Valentine's new song "Social Apocalypse." I know Bullet's biggest songs pretty well, but I'm not a hardcore fan who's listened to every album and deep cut. If YouTube Music had randomly dropped Social Apocalypse into one of my playlists without me knowing who it was, especially during that instrumental opening, I would've had to pull out my phone and check who was playing. Nothing about it would've immediately made me think "oh, this is Bullet." I've seen other people say the new song doesn't have that signature Bullet sound, while more dedicated fans say they can absolutely hear Bullet in it, especially similarities to certain eras. That's where I started wondering if this "fingerprint" doesn't exist entirely in the music. Maybe part of it exists in the listener too. I've listened to basically everything Breaking Benjamin has released, so my brain has a huge sample of what Breaking Benjamin sounds like. My idea of Bullet comes from a much smaller sample, mostly their biggest songs. Someone who knows every Bullet record might hear connections in Social Apocalypse that I simply don't have the reference points to recognize. Changing singers makes it even weirder. Killswitch Engage still sounds like Killswitch to me with either Jesse Leach or Howard Jones. Three Days Grace kept a lot of what made them recognizable after Adam Gontier left, but at the same time they had obviously lost one of the most recognizable parts of their sound. And now Linkin Park with Emily Armstrong has me thinking about the same thing. Chester Bennington's voice was a massive part of Linkin Park's identity, but it clearly wasn't the only thing that made Linkin Park sound like Linkin Park. Then you have Falling in Reverse, where I'm not even sure genre is very useful for identifying the band anymore. "Ronald," "All My Life," "Watch the World Burn," and their version of "Last Resort" go in completely different directions, but somehow there's still an identity connecting them. Even the whole "djent isn't a genre, it's a technique" argument made me think about this. Historically, sure. But if somebody describes a band as djent, most metal listeners probably imagine a hell of a lot more than one guitar technique. Certain tones, low tunings, rhythms, production styles, extended-range guitars, etc. have all become associated with that word to the point where it describes a recognizable sound whether you want to call it a genre or not. That seems weirdly similar to what I'm talking about. Our brains take a bunch of individual musical traits and eventually start recognizing the combination as something. The simplest way I've been able to describe it is: Genre is the neighborhood a song lives in. Technique is part of the toolbox used to make it. A band's fingerprint is whatever makes you recognize who built it. I'm not claiming "fingerprint" is an actual music theory term or that I've figured any of this out. It's just the best way I've found to describe something I've apparently been doing subconsciously for years. So I'm curious how other people experience this. What actually creates a band's fingerprint for you? Is it something that's just there in the music, or is part of it something our brains learn from listening to a band over time? And what are some bands that have changed dramatically but somehow still sound like themselves? Or the opposite, bands that stayed in roughly the same genre but stopped sounding like themselves to you?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Were They Might Be Giants revolutionaries? Were They Might Be Giants actually kind of revolutionary? This is something I’ve been thinking about lately: They Might Be Giants have always struck me as much more musically and lyrically radical than their presentation would suggest. On the surface, they can sound almost aggressively harmless: goofy, nerdy, understated, lo-fi-ish, melodic, and often deliberately silly. There’s no obvious rock-star posturing, no grandiose sense of importance, and very little of the “we are changing the world” attitude that usually accompanies the word revolutionary . A lot of their songs sound like little jokes, observations, children's songs, absurdist sketches, or deliberately trivial pieces of pop music. But that's almost the point. Their songwriting has this very strange combination of rationality, absurdity, sarcasm, deadpan humor, and genuine musical craft . They can take something completely ridiculous and present it with the seriousness of a scientific observation — or take something mundane and make it sound bizarre simply by looking at it from an unexpected angle. Songs like Particle Man , Istanbul (Not Constantinople) , Birdhouse in Your Soul , Don't Let's Start , Ana Ng , She's an Angel , The Statue Got Me High , etc. don't necessarily sound revolutionary in the traditional sense. But they seem to have helped establish a vocabulary for a kind of alternative songwriting where being clever, weird, funny, emotionally detached, and poppy could all coexist . And I wonder if their influence becomes more obvious when you compare them to a lot of post-2000 indie music. A huge amount of modern indie has that somewhat towned-down, understated, self-aware, sardonic quality. The vocals are often deliberately un-grand, the arrangements can be simple or slightly twee, the lyrics can be observational or ironic, and there's often a kind of “I'm making a song about this ridiculous little thing because why not?” attitude. Obviously, TMBG didn't invent irony, nerdiness, lo-fi music, quirky songwriting, or indie pop. And there are plenty of other artists who were doing similar things before them. But they seem like an unusually early and concentrated example of something that later became much more normal in alternative/indie music: the idea that you don't have to be cool, macho, tortured, profound, or conventionally “rock” to make sophisticated music. What's especially interesting to me is that their silliness doesn't necessarily make the music less sophisticated. In some ways, the silliness gives them more freedom. They can jump between genres, structures, lyrical perspectives, and subjects without having to maintain a serious artistic persona. So I'm wondering: were They Might Be Giants actually more musically/culturally revolutionary than they get credit for? Not “revolutionary” in the political sense, obviously, but revolutionary in the sense that they helped normalize a particular kind of intellectual, absurdist, sarcastic, deliberately uncool, pop-oriented indie songwriting . Or am I retroactively giving them too much credit because their style happens to resemble a lot of indie music that came later? I'm especially curious how people who listened to them in the '80s and '90s perceived them at the time. Did they feel genuinely weird and groundbreaking then, or did they mostly just seem like a particularly funny/quirky alternative band?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Lulu by Lou Reed ft. Metallica is a masterpiece and a worthy sendoff to one of the greatest songwriters and wordsmiths of our time. David Bowie famously expressed his admiration for Lulu by proclaiming it a masterpiece and Lou’s best work – and I agree to a large extent, although it seems that this remains contrary to popular opinion.  I often still find Lulu frequenting lists of “worst albums of all time” on the web, and I guess that’s understandable because it’s not a pleasant album – far from it.  In fact, it is a difficult, bizarre, depraved, morbid, long and sometimes inscrutable, yet endlessly intriguing Frankenstein of an album.  It can be a lot to take in and not everybody is willing to take the plunge in its deep, bloody waters.  Just like the music of Captain Beefheart, Syd Barret, Throbbing Gristle, Swans and other artists whose works do not lend themselves to easy pigeonholing, this album sounds like nothing else in music history and is steeped deep in the avant-garde.  You either like it or you don’t if it’s not your thing. But I think it’s unfair to call it one of the worst albums ever made just because it’s not for you. To say that Lulu is not an album made to appeal to mainstream tastes is an understatement. It explores uncomfortable themes that are too extreme for a lot of people, even metalheads. But if you happen to like weird, darkly experimental and extreme music with depth, there is a lot of joy to be had beneath the apparently disgusting, bloody, grimy and shit-covered surface. Underneath it all, there is a light, a peculiar wisdom, a state of grace, coming from the big, coagulating heart of Lou Reed whose true capacity for love is so great that it can find the good, the beautiful and the worthy even in the worst aspects of human life. This is music made for the contemplative type of listener who likes thought-provoking stuff and a good challenge – not to mention outright weirdos and freaks on the kinky side of the spectrum. It rewards deep, repeated listens and commands intense loyalty from those who have already fallen deeply in love with it.

text: 'Becoming Led Zeppelin' - How times have changed! Watched this last night -- very entertaining for a life-long Zep fan. One thing that got me thinking, though, was the way in which their initial success in America was framed: Radio stations at the time were in the habit of playing the entire A-side of an album, give a short announce and an ad break, then come back to play the B-side! Maybe not mainstream commercial radio, but certainly college radio and local stations... but the point is that enough kids were listening for it have a massive impact, given that they were touring heavily at the same time. Obviously, it didn't hurt that they had Atlantic distributing the records, and Jimmy Page / The Yardbirds reputation was strong enough that the gigs they booked were in major venues... plus they were in a position to bankroll the whole operation. Still, what struck me is the idea of people actually hearing whole albums on the radio! How does that compare with today, where you're lucky to get the attention span of a gnat on social media, and 30-second shorts are where it's at? Despite having 'the goods' in every conceivable sense, I actually find it hard to imagine that any band could do what Zeppelin did back in the late 60s today. Or, to put it another way, I would say that if the equivalent of Led Zeppelin landed today, they would be at best a band that 'some people' have heard of and certainly not the global phenomenon that they so quickly became.

text: As a longtime fan of both projects, I only just pondered on how similar the career trajectories of Swans and Godflesh have been. Godflesh's latest album Decay was released yesterday, their 10th studio full-length and the 4th since their comeback in 2014 after a 13 year hiatus. What started as raw and angry sound that pioneered the industrial metal genre was later refined into an equally abrasive and heavy style but with more maturity and experimentation, combining elements from softer genres like shoegaze and electronica into their heavily down-tuned style. In tandem with this shift of direction, the themes in their lyrics, written mostly by founder/frontman Justin K Broadrick, went from corruption, nihilism, and hatred from the eyes of a young brit to a more introspective view on the world, inner self, and death, brought forth from one who experienced all hardships of life and the wisdom it provides. Despite their differences in sound, the path of Michael Gira and his band Swans wasn't so different. Started back in the early 80s apart of the NYC No Wave scene, Swan's early works were just as abrasive, noisy, experimental and angry, with their first four albums being straight industrial noise rock before adding experimentations of other sounds into their sound. Their comeback album in 2010 My Father Will Guide Me Up a Rope to the Sky marked the end of a 14 year hiatus, and while not considered as remarkable compared to the other new-era albums like The Seer and To Be Kind , was still met with positive reception and excitement that their return was going to be long-term, eventually proving true. Their sound became noticeably more mature in style and concept, focusing on arrangement of a larger palette of instruments, motifs, and repetition with themes of spirituality anchoring the album's theme while maintaining a loud, powerful sound that would later be dubbed as the "Big Sound" era of Swans. What once were two young entities dispelling their anger with society from different sides of the world, grew older and much wiser, reflecting on the hardships and experiences of life which reflected in their evolving sounds. It's not easy for bands to take a 10+ year long hiatus and come back with not only the same intensity but with an even greater following than the first half of their careers, but both projects achieved just that, furthering their influence and legacies as some of the best experimental projects to have ever been created. While Broadrick has come out and announced this latest album will mark the beginning of the end for the project, it's hard to say whether or not Swans will also be winding down too due to Gira's age, but without any indication from the latter to be substantiated, both acts left an incredible footprint on music as a whole for generations to come.

text: Sophisti-pop, and other genres that have never had a revival One of my favorite musical discoveries in the last decade was Sophisti-pop. While the name is a bit, frankly, not great, the genre itself is absolutely stacked full of critically acclaimed artists and albums. Artists like China Crisis, Roxy Music, Prefab Sprout, Everything but the Girl's early work, Level 42, and my personal favorite, The Blue Nile. It's a very specific sound, and it emerged at a very specific point in time. It got moderately to very popular, depending on the artist (Sade was massive, for instance), but for all intents and purposes only practically existed between 1982 or 83 to around 1990, and fizzled back into the underground after. While other artists have played with this sound on songs here and there, like Blood Orange and Carly Rae Jepsen, it's never had a true revival at any point in time. So that got me thinking: What other notable 20 th century styles of music have never had a popular revival, even for a short period of time? Obviously, this isn't focused on a song or two that might have come out, but proper revivals, such as the swing and rockabilly revival in the mid 90's, or the disco and funk revival that happened at the end of the 2010's into the early 2020's.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Alexander Bard's many groups Alexander Bard is a Swedish producer and composer whose career in music has spanned for nearly four decades now. Throughout that time, he has created not less than four groups - Army of Lovers, Vaccum, Bodies Without Organs, and Gravitonas - and created a bunch of songs for other groups, such as Crying At The Discoteque for Alcazar. I've heard many songs from all these groups, as they were considerably popular in my country and I personally like most of them. I'm not musically trained at all, but even to me it is clear that the absolute majority of all songs from all these groups pertain to the pop genre. They are easy on the ears, they are often catchy. Not only that, but they all feel like they have been made by the same person or a collection of people. That is, of course, because they are all ultimately made by Bard himself, more or less. The one distinctive feature I can note with all my non-existent musical expertise is that many bridges in his songs feature lyrics, often in a voice distinctly different from the overall sound of the song, or even in a different language. What I don't get is why Bard made so many groups if he continues to pump out the same sort of product through all of them (I'm pretty sure most of the music and lyrics are either his own or approved by him - he seems to be quite egotistical and unlikely to let anyone control the direction). It's not like those groups fell apart - Army of Lovers presented a new banger and a whole album a couple of years ago, Vaccum and Gravitonas apparently still exist. So why so many groups? What's the goal of creating a collection of bands if the music, in its core, stays the same throughout?
label: Deep Analysis

text: In my humble opinion " The heart of Saturday night"whole album is very underrated. I feel like The Heart of Saturday Night gets kinda slept on when people talk about Tom Waits. Everyone always brings up Closing Time for the pure singer-songwriter stuff, then Nighthawks at the Diner and Small Change when they want the full beatnik, whiskey-soaked Tom Waits experience. And obviously Rain Dogs gets brought up in basically every “best Tom Waits album” discussion. But The Heart of Saturday Night? Feels like it gets treated as just a stepping stone to the stuff that came later.And honestly, going back to it lately, I think that’s a bit unfair. This album is so damn good. What gets me most is the atmosphere. It has this really specific late-night, working-class kinda feeling to it. The production by Bones Howe is warm and laid-back, and with Jim Hughart’s bass and Pete Christlieb’s sax, the whole thing sounds like you're sitting alone in some shitty little diner at 2 AM, drinking coffee while neon lights are reflecting off the wet street outside. You know the vibe. Then there’s the songwriting. You can really hear the Beat poetry influence starting to take shape. “Diamonds on My Windshield” and “New Coat of Paint” basically feel like Kerouac got turned into a jazz record. There’s this whole sense of driving around at night with nowhere particularly important to be, just taking in the city and letting your thoughts wander. And then you get “San Diego Serenade” and the title track, which honestly might be two of the most beautiful and straightforward songs he ever wrote. No weird gimmicks, no over-the-top gravelly Tom Waits persona, just great melodies and ridiculously good lyrics. I think that’s probably what I love most about the album. It captures this little window where Waits still sounds warm and hopeful, even when there’s that underlying loneliness. You can almost hear the darker, grittier version of him that's gonna show up later, but he hasn't completely disappeared into that character yet. It doesn’t scream for your attention like some of his later records do. It just kinda sits there and does its thing. Or maybe im just a 23 years old rambling about a bygone era album  and not seeing it get enough love.
label: Deep Analysis

text: I really love The Unforgettable Fire by U2! Finally revisited a couple of U2 albums during this weekend. Went back to Boy, War & The Unforgettable Fire yesterday, and I tried The Joshua Tree today. Loved all of them, but the one that stood out to me the most is The Unforgettable Fire. It is absolutely a massive left turn in comparison to Boy & War for example. Tunes such as “Sunday Bloody Sunday”, “Like a Song” & “Seconds” were pissed off - politically charged with a visceral element & a very angry feel. Tough and gritty, like an activist who’s completely committed to spreading their message & unafraid to say “go kick some rocks” if necessary. And I felt that Boy was full of this youthful exuberance. Wide-eyed with a bit of a punk edge to it. Whereas right off of the bat, The Unforgettable Fire is completely different. Dreamy, ethereal, blurry & hazy. Closer to what I’d expect from ambient music with a ton of straight up psychedelic touches. More introspective rather than intense. And I love that! I feel that The Unforgettable Fire is the closest that U2 ever got to Cocteau Twins. All of that textured & atmospheric guitar work & the emphasis on beautiful/otherworldly sounds. Some of that album’s layers reminded me of what Wire accomplished on 154 as well. I even picked up some elements of Krautrock (specifically CAN/NEU! maybe)? I think it’s so cool how U2’s biiiiig, bold, anthemic style was translated into a more foggy & surreal vibe on The Unforgettable Fire. The songs aren’t as tightly woven as The Joshua Tree, but I think it’s a strength. There’s something about The Unforgettable Fire’s more impressionistic style that really resonates with me. Definitely an album that I could play during an afternoon walk in December, with snow everywhere & a chilly breeze running through my fingers. Amazing album overall. I actually prefer it to The Joshua Tree :)
label: Deep Analysis

text: Do you prefer a more natural sounding mix or a heavily produced and polished one? I've been thinking a lot about production lately. text: Is there an asymmetry to how music critics discuss “simple” and “complex” music? Technical virtuosity and emotional expression are often considered mutually exclusive ideas. I disagree. I would actually posit that prog, jazz, metal, or otherwise maximalist musicians are actually deeply passionate about what they do, often have something unique and profound to say, and are choosing to express themselves with a more advanced form of language, much like poets or playwrights. And rather than attacking the language outright, we should grant these musicians the same grace we extend to three-chord singer-songwriters and ambient synthesists, who are often considered more “honest” artists. What critics call “bloat” can actually serve distinct artistic purposes: Long-form composition can signify a vast journey, literally or metaphorically, and allow the writers ample time for motivic development. Shifting key centers or time signatures can indicate changes in mood or atmosphere. Use of atypical or mixed modes can communicate an unusual or “outsider” perspective. Maximalist arranging can take already large emotions and make them overwhelming. Exceeding the established limitations of musical convention can communicate a deep spiritual transcendence. And yet, often when an artist shows a level of ambition beyond what is “cool,” they are often hit with lazy shorthand words like “overwrought,” “self-indulgent,” or the worst offender “masturbatory.” Conversely, minimalism is granted profundity by default. Restraint is always seen as a sign of “maturity.” Records with a lot of emptier space leave a considerable amount of room for the listener to project their own feelings, increasing a sense of depth that may or may not already be there. This leads to a broader follow-up question: Should paid professional music critics have a better understanding of concepts like composition, arranging, and musicianship? Consider the absurdity of an NFL sportswriter who doesn't know the basic rules and regulations of football; or a food critic who couldn’t distinguish between common cooking methods or ingredients. Why do we allow music critics to feel everything out on vibes instead of insisting that they show a firm understanding about the building blocks of their chosen medium? EDIT: Really appreciate all the thoughtful and insightful replies here, whether we agreed or disagreed. I'm stepping away now, so if you reply to get a final word in, I guess it's the final word. text: Low listening minutes. Is everyone else constantly listening to music in the background? In college I lived on campus (no commute) and I barely had any free time outside of studying and other responsibilities so that left me with about an hour a day to listen to music. I also don't like being on AUX so my music was never the background music when hanging out. On top of listening on Spotify, I also spend a lot of time playing guitar, piano and drums and singing. That and my daily commute are without a doubt going to be reflected this year in my listening stats. text: Has music become less "daring" over the last years/decades? A few days ago, I asked myself the question if music had become less "daring" over the last decades, and I wondered if I just feel this, or if others feel this way too. But first, I want to explain how this question arised. Let us go back in time, back to the early 1960s. Rock'n'Roll was the big deal over in America, but then suddenly, a new group in the UK arises, breaking with a lot of traditions and typical ideas about music. I am talking about "The Beatles". The Beatles are among my favourite artists, and Revolver and Abbey Road are my favourite Beatles albums. Revolver was quite unique, too. A reversed guitar solo, tape effects etc. Only a few years later, prog-bands like King Crimson, ELP, Yes, Genesis and CAN emerged. They all pushed the boundaries of rock music in different directions. King Crimson especially in their 70s with LTIA and Red (but of course also in the 80s with their new-wave style), Yes and ELP in other, yet also not less interesting and "new" territories. At the same time, Germany brought out electronic music bands like Tangerine Dream and Kraftwerk, who both significantly shaped this new genre, while being successfull. Then, we had bands like Nirvana, that managed to make a more underground genre (grunge) popular, and became successfull. I could go on and list a lot of other artists, who didn't stick to the same musical ideas throughout their career, like Kate Bush, Tool, Talk Talk and of course David Bowie. And while we may have an Angine de Poitrine in 2026, artists which want to break out of established musical constructs have become a rarity, at least, those who are still somewhat successfull while doing this. If all of this is really true, and that music has become less courageous, one question still remains: why? What caused all of this to happen? Is it the omnipresent availabilty of music via streaming services? I don't know. I'd really be interested in how you see this.
label: Deep Analysis

text: The Foxes and almost making it Hi all, Has anyone ever heard of a band from the UK called The Foxes? They came out around 2006 and were an indie rock band. It was MySpace, after all, where you could just comment on a bands page and sometimes they’d just reply. On more than one occasion their singer, Nigel, responded to me. I remember them posting about potentially doing a US tour and while I never was able to go myself, they did do the tour. I found out recently that Nigel has been posting on [Substack](https://substack.com/@nigelthomaswriter?r=7unuck&utm_medium=ios&utm_source=stories&shareImageVariant=image) detailing the start of the band, getting scouted, being featured on MySpace and he’s currently up to the US Tour part of the story which I am so incredibly interested in since I didn’t get to experience it while it was happening! It’s fascinating seeing the process of « making it » through the bands eyes. Really unique, especially when I compare where I was at the time (ie encountering them on MySpace) versus his retelling of what was happening from the bands perspective. He’s also a wonderful writer. The way he tells it is entertaining and so very well thought out. He even includes diary entries - always humourous! Has anyone else ever seen something like this from a band? The behind the scenes bits are fascinating. I’d love to see if any other bands have done or written something similar? He still makes himself accessible for comments and things which blows me away. So unlike most bands I’ve seen. I feel like I’m always alone in knowing about them. Just curious if anyone else knows who they are? Anyone listened to them? Came across them on the myspace featured artists page? I’m so surprised they never took off here more, especially since I remember Franz Ferdinand being pretty well known! Oh, incase nobody knows what I’m talking about — check them out. They haven’t been together for years and years but I keep them on my playlist. If you’re into the mid 2000s post punk/indie scene from the UK give them a [listen.](https://youtube.com/@thefoxes?si=1FEKS8-dX7oDzvdR) My favourites are Lover, Killer and Trauma Town, personally !

When I hear a new band that people describe as post-punk, their sound hits you over the head with angst and distorted bass lines and crushed drums. I think a long enough time has passed to where the new sound is its own thing, and the original era can be cemented in the history books as the movement that actually changed music. Most of what you think of when you say "80s music" is that nerdy but vibrant brand of catchy hooks and drum machines that arrived after the rise of punk and the fall of disco. text: Why does nobody seem to notice how bad Prince sounds? I think he's a fine musician, but I've never much liked him because I can't get over how incredibly low-fidelity so many of his recordings are. I remember returning a used vinyl copy of 1999 once because I couldn't believe how damaged it was, only to listen to it on CD years later and realize that it was just that the recording sounded exactly like a worn-out record. Same with much from Purple Rain, Let's Go Crazy sounds so tinny and awful. I know why it is, I've read up on it - it's because he recorded so much in his home studio, he had bad discipline about bouncing tracks and it incurred a ton of generation loss. What I can't work out is how this isn't commented on more. Outside of some talk on audiophile forums this just seems to have gone unnoticed by the listening public. And it's not something like Springsteen's Nebraska where the low-fidelity production adds to the aesthetic, either - the sound he's going for is actively impaired by the production, and things improve massively when he starts focusing more on instruments from Parade on. Has anyone else noticed this, and if so, why do you think more people haven't? Am I too sensitive or is he just that good of a songwriter?
label: Deep Analysis

text: The anniversary of "Nevermind" has remind me how we don't have course corrections anymore Nevermind and grunge represented ideals like danger, authenticity, recklessness, rebellion, controversy, etc, that shook things up every so often, eg, punk, as a backlash towards the mainstream when things got too formulaic We hit a wall and the bubble eventually bursts. We no longer see this with algorithms, the Internet, social media, the music industry, etc. All that has died. Someone actually pointed out that grunge might be less of a music revolution and more of a "course correction". We haven't had one of these over the past few decades...and we're actually beginning to see the product of this. It's allowed culture to be stagnant...like a pond festering. And when there is no shake up--like a stone being thrown--The Machine controls things, monopoly on music, insane concert prices, dopamine decadence, aging rockers, prepackaged music, There's an entire demographic that has never experienced this music/cultural shift, so I wouldn't rely on the generation driving culture to change things. But we really could use one of these again. A reset. A course correction.

text: Does the novelty of obscure music matter to you? Does the obscurity competition for music feel tiring? On the one hand, I think it does make sense to dig for under-the-radar works and artists. There's an inherent appeal and novelty in discovering music that hasn't come across your radar at any point prior. Or finding music that isn't easily accessible through the radio or streaming. There may be a sense of pride in having independent initiative rather than having something seemingly fed to you. Crate digging has been a popular pastime for decades as well as giving material for artists to sample and/or re-contextualize. On an identity level, it's been a status symbol to be ahead of the curve in appreciating artists before the majority of the population or liking an artist that maybe not everyone else likes. On the other hand, I've wondered if it can feel tiring to keep up with finding the most obscure music and artists. Maybe you've had those flashbacks or even discussions where a music fan will act like an artist/work is more obscure than they actually are. Then from another direction, there will be a mentality where "true obscurity" is a particular standard that one has to reach and dig for while everything else is "too mainstream". With the availability of music on online platforms, file-sharing, and evolving values like encouraging people to share and archive rather than hoarding for yourself, it seems like obscurity is not only shrinking (though there are certainly exceptions, lots of music history hasn't been documented) but less desirable in the first place. After all, if you find something, many would encourage wider knowledge rather than hiding things away to keep others ignorant. I know some commenters will go "I like all kinds of good music, doesn't matter if it's popular or underground". But overall, I'm wondering if the idea of finding music that's obscure matters to you.
label: Philosophical Discussion

The marquee song would be 3rd or 4th in the order. You had no choice but listen to 1st, 2nd song as the process of fast-forwarding was tedious and imperfect. But over period of time you start appreciating the other tracks for their own merit. Some tracks have a peculiar music arrangement that appeal to you, some have vocals that struck the right chord. For some you develop a liking not for no particular reason. Some tracks become ear-worms and when you are doing something else and you cannot place it but it hits you that the track was present on that particular album, over period of time all the songs make a place for themselves. I had a similar experience recently with an album called Hurry Up, We Are Dreaming by M83. I was not aware of existence of this band. It popped up on Reddit. The title seemed interesting to me. I had no notion of what kind of music or genre this album belonged to. I started listening to the album during transit. Initial tracks did not appeal to me until I reached a particular track, ‘Raconte-moi une histoire’ . The voice of small girl telling a story about frog, an Alice in wonderland kind of story, hooked me. So I went on listening to whole track. Again next few tracks did not hold my attention until the one called ‘Year One, One UFO’ . The music arrangement with sparing use of chant more mesmerising. It hit me the heart next to the mark immediately. On 3rd and 4th listen I appreciated the other tracks like ‘My Tears Are Becoming a Sea’, ‘Soon, My Friend’ , and rest of the songs. This journey of getting to know an album, getting familiar with some songs and then falling in love with some and extension of whole album is something I started thinking about.

text: Is "Revolution 9" by The Beatles their most visionary "song"? "Revolution 9" by The Beatles is one of the most unique, odd, and polarizing tracks in their discography. I, like many people, used to hate it and always treated it as an easy skip when listening to The White Album . Recently, however, I have developed a newfound appreciation for it. I would now argue that "Revolution 9" is one of the most innovative and visionary pieces the band ever created. How can a track so universally disliked become a respected piece of art to an individual? And I am certainly not the only one who defends it. I think of "Revolution 9" as less of a traditional song and more of an experience, acting as a sonic and atmospheric painting. Of course, music is subjective, and this perspective doesn't mean you have to enjoy it. I will be the first to admit that I don't listen to it the way I would a regular track. You can't just listen for melody, chords, or a standard beat. Instead, it is much closer to visual art. I would compare its ambient, atmospheric walls of sound to modern post-rock and electronic artists like Boards of Canada, Godspeed You! Black Emperor, and Aphex Twin. A great conceptual parallel to this track is the album Everywhere at the End of Time by The Caretaker. This project refuses to be simplified into basic pop music. The album sonically mirrors the ongoing battle with dementia, charting the incremental degradation of a mind through fleeting memories and building confusion. As it progresses, the audio becomes hollow, fractured, and decayed. You don't casually say, "Hey, I want to listen to that dementia album." You sit with it as if you were staring at a painting. To me, "Revolution 9" evokes a similar, heavy conceptual weight. It sounds like the auditory experience of suffering a traumatic brain injury, or perhaps the final moments of dying. It captures a consciousness becoming fragmented, overwhelmed, and completely detached from ordinary reality. You hear the fleeting final moments of life through distorting voices, repetitious loops, and abstract thoughts. It sounds like a mind fleeing from life, being forgotten, and degrading back to its primordial self. In my opinion, that makes it one of the most visionary "songs" in The Beatles' entire catalog.
