Is it such an inconvenience to delete an album off your device that it'd forever negatively taint their reputation? Personally, I thoroughly enjoyed everything until How To Dismantle An Atomic Bomb - actually, that and All That You Can't Leave Behind are my favourite U2 albums- granted, I think it's because they're the two I grew up with. And I even liked No Line On The Horizon , but that seems to never be talked about. It was definitely the album/moment where they quite heavily began to veer off into "phoning it in" territory. I'm sure some would argue that happened with my two favourite albums I mentioned above, but obviously my bias won't let me say that. I genuinely, thoroughly, enjoy almost every track on those two records. They make epic feel-good music which so many love and can vibe out to together, and there's great value in that, imo. Again, I'm obviously biased, but I genuinely can't fathom why the endless hate. It's funny when people will spew endless hate on them but always have the caveat "but their first few albums..."- it's just funny to observe the switch-up, from loving something to hating it so strongly. Moby is another one... I don't actually know whether he was actually widely loved or always kind of made fun of... I want to say Eminem alone did irreparable damage to the perception of Moby lol...but like, it seemed somewhat okay to say you liked him in the 2000's, whereas now, you're made to be some big lame if you do. As much as I'm for animal rights and don't deny his heart is in the right place with all that, it can definitely be heavy-handed and over-the-top. RHCP another one, similar to U2, where the first few albums, culminating in BSSM, are seen as something revolutionary/explosive/amazing, but anything later gets regularly put down. My personal favourite is the three record run of Californication-By The Way-Stadium Arcadium . Coldplay... they seemed to be made fun of from the start, for what, allegedly being a Radiohead rip-off/wannabe? Idk, they're def nowhere near Radiohead quality/status, but their first three or four albums are solid. I will admit, even as a fan, that anything post-Mylo Xyloto (and even that album) just sounds so overtly polished and devoid of soul. A big departure from the first few. See, even just writing all this out, I can already feel your hate and judgement coming a mile away, I've been so conditioned to be ashamed of my taste by fellow music fans, which is what the real lame thing is, imo. I'm just curious though what it is that makes certain once-loved acts become hated later. And I mean purely as far as the music goes- of course with the shitty things they've done in their personal lives, that's more than reason enough to forever hate on someone... but this hate was observed before many such things came to light- like there was some collective barometer reading "sellout". text: Molly Hatchet is kind of fun. For decades I've seen Molly Hatchet albums at second-hand stores and never, not even once, was curious about what they sounded like. As someone that grew up in a place with ZERO rock on the radio (country, tejano and a top 40 station that included hits in Spanish). I learned about classic rock later in life and just assumed that maybe that was a Charlie Daniels Band song. I was exposed to MTV rock, but classic rock? Nope. It was so bad I would tape rock stations when I went out of town just to hear something different. If you like southern, twangy, over the top bluesy rock that whole album is amazing. The song Fall of the Peacekeepers is pretty amazing as well from a different album. It turns out that at least that whole Flirtin' with Disaster album is a good time. Overly technical southern rock with more freewheeling solos than necessary. You get a feeling, especially because they're from Florida, some of these guys would be in technical death metal bands today due to how complex the guitar game is. It's fun. It's party music for the most part. Also, this band is a total mess when it comes to who is even in the band and what they were up to. They are touring right now and no original members are still alive. Total Madness. I don't know if they've had more lineup changes than Napalm Death or TSOL. There's absolutely no reason for a wiki page to be this long. I kind of wish Danny McBride would star in a movie about these guys. They started off as a cover band that would just play every club in Jacksonville and then change the band name and do it all over again. They also sounded so much like Lynyrd Skynyrd that a member of LS was on the verge of heading into the studio with them when the plane crash happened. Anyway, just wanted to post something fun and talk about a bunch of crazy southern guys making music that anyone born below the Mason Dixon line will be naturally drawn to. Something about that twangy sound that will get to you if your from the South, makes me think of Bret Hinds and his bluegrass pickin' solos on all those Mastodon albums. text: Why are bands with truly shared male-female lead vocals so uncommon? I’ve been thinking about how unusual it feels for a pop or rock band to have male and female members who both function as genuine lead singers. Not just one person getting a song or two, but a setup where switching between voices is core to the band’s identity. Wussy is probably my favorite example. Both Chuck Cleaver and Lisa Walker write and sing a substantial share of the material, and that contrast feels essential to what the band is. There are a few other cases like X, Stars, and The xx, and I think I’d put Fleetwood Mac at the low end of what I consider a true shared split of vocal duties. Bands like Sonic Youth and Yo La Tengo thus don’t quite make the cut for me, but some may disagree there. (The B-52s might fit, but I’m not sure how they share duties outside the radio singles.) If I’m not missing too many bands, this dynamic is comparatively rare. Why is that? Is it industry pressure for one identifiable front person, or patterns in who writes songs? Two voices seem to open up different narrative and emotional space without changing the band’s core sound. Really curious what factors might be at work here.
label: Philosophical Discussion

At the same time, there are plenty of examples of artists who took big creative risks and still landed massive successes: Miley herself with Plastic Hearts , Madonna with Ray of Light , Taylor Swift with Folklore , and Beyoncé with Renaissance . This isn’t about whether those albums deserved more recognition. It’s about figuring out why some experiments work and others don’t. Is it just about quality? text: Where do you draw the line between late ’60s heavy rock and the first true heavy metal hit? Some of the earliest contenders for the first heavy metal hit single have something surprising in common: they were covers of pop hits. In 1968, Blue Cheer transformed Eddie Cochran’s “Summertime Blues” into a wall of distorted guitar, thunderous bass and pounding drums. Their version reached #14 on the Hot 100. That same year, Vanilla Fudge took The Supremes’ #1 hit “You Keep Me Hangin’ On,” slowed it dramatically and turned it into something much darker and heavier. Then Deep Purple reinvented Billy Joe Royal’s “Hush” with a heavier psychedelic sound and took it all the way to #4. Of course, there are other contenders. The Kinks had “You Really Got Me” in 1964. Then came Steppenwolf, Cream, Iron Butterfly and The Beatles’ “Helter Skelter.” But maybe none of these are actually heavy metal. Maybe they’re better classified as heavy rock or proto-metal , with heavy metal as a distinct genre truly beginning with Black Sabbath. That’s the part I find interesting. What separates heavy rock or proto-metal from actual heavy metal for you? And does any pre-Sabbath hit cross that line?
label: Deep Analysis

When rumours start, artists are expected to speak on the matter, defend themselves, confirm or deny the rumours. And whenever an artist doesn't, they're dragged through the mud. My best example of 2026 is Miss Tate McRae. People have been so after Tate lately because she won't speak on personal matters. Because she's not selling her personality or private life, she's selling her music and artist skills. text: Did the 1992 EMI takeover of Virgin (and the death of the Singles chart) systematically kill off good new bands in the 90s? I’ve run into a massive roadblock with 1990s music, and I’m trying to figure out if corporate consolidation is structurally to blame for it. I am a massive fan of late 70s and 80s bands, particularly from the UK and Australia. My absolute favorites are Depeche Mode, The Chameleons, Crowded House, and The Railway Children. I especially love the albums Black Celebration, Strange Times, Temple of Low Men and Native Place (1990). The only 90s band I’ve genuinely connected with is the Australian group The Whitlams. I know the common culprits: the physical vinyl format practically vanished for casual buyers, and there was a massive industry shift away from the traditional Singles charts toward long-form, album-oriented CDs. But I’m curious about the back-end corporate shift. Thorn EMI bought Virgin Records in 1992, which was essentially the last massive independent major label. Did this specific buyout—and the subsequent corporate consolidation of the 90s—directly kill the market for bands who relied on that specific 80s melodic/single architecture? Did major labels corporate-streamline their rosters, pulling funding from mid-tier atmospheric bands to dump all their money into global pop or cookie-cutter Grunge/Britpop clones? I'd love to hear thoughts on how the industry restructuring of the early 90s altered what actually got distributed. EDIT: Wrap-Up & Key Takeaways from the Comments This thread exploded. Thank you for the incredible insights. Based on the 90+ comments, here is the final synthesis of how the 1990s music ecosystem actually shifted: - SoundScan was the smoking gun. The mid-1991 introduction of automated barcode tracking changed everything. It replaced subjective store reports with raw data. - The "Opening Weekend" corporate mentality. SoundScan proved alternative rock, hip-hop, and country moved immediate units. Corporate boards shifted to a brutal data-driven paradigm. If an album didn't explode instantly, labels pulled funding. - Roster purges of mid-tier talent. The 1992 corporate takeovers (like EMI absorbing Virgin) streamlined the industry. Labels aggressively purged beautiful, idiosyncratic, mid-tier musical architecture. UK and Australian acts like The Railway Children , The Blue Aeroplanes , The Hummingbirds , and Girl Overboard were dropped overnight. - Sonic real estate vs. compositional architecture. Major 90s albums weren't cheap to engineer. Budgets were massive for bands like Oasis or Smashing Pumpkins. But corporate money moved away from diverse instrumentation (strings, horns, session players). Instead, cash paid for compression to make standard rock setups sound massive. - A highly standardized 90s monoculture. The industry used data to scale a predictable formula. This left music fans with three stark choices: multi-platinum corporate flagships, underground indie-label darlings, or highly compressed radio rock. For those who valued melodic depth, textured arrangements, and sophisticated studio songwriting over raw angst and distortion, the post-1992 corporate machine didn't just change the charts—it systematically dismantled the architecture required for our favourite genres to survive. Thank you to everyone who contributed to this discussion! With 90+ comments, we’ve covered everything from SoundScan data to the corporate restructuring of 1992. I'm officially signing off from this thread now. Appreciate the incredible insights and debates!

text: Shared musical culture and shared audio environments This is something I've been mulling over since a post a few weeks back about monoculture, and whether it ever really existed or not. When talking about monoculture(s) or shared cultures we tend to talk about gatekeepers and the availability of music. A small number of labels controlling what gets played on the radio, a few TV channels with limited music programming, the cost and availability of records... What I think is often overlooked is how people's audio environment has become more individual. That's a fancy way of saying something very simple. When we're around other people we're less likely to be listening to the same things as them, and we're around other people less in the first place. In the past, if you had a family gathered in a room they'd likely all have to hear the TV (or radio or hi-fi) even if they were doing something else. Now it's much easier for people to be absorbed in their own thing via their laptop/tablet/phone, with their own audio environment. Or perhaps you're out shopping with your headphones in rather than hearing the music that's playing in shops and shopping centres (or you're not going our shopping at all, you're ordering online). Maybe you're talking to or playing games with friends - but instead of being in the same space, you're all in different places, listening to different things. Of course, this isn't new (you could probably take it as far back as the grammaphone (edit: I don't think I've ever written the word "gramophone" before) but it's also much more prevalent than it used to be. It's probably also enhanced by noise cancelling headphones and (more low-tech) by the predominance of earplug-like earbuds. I might also suggest that this line of thinking can help us identify exceptions to the rule. I assume just about everyone here knows Baby Shark? (do doo doo-doo-do-do.) Obviously there are a bunch of reasons for that, but one is that if you're around small children, then you can't avoid hearing the things they like. I do wonder if there are other examples like this that might prove the rule.
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: Copyright Act of 1909 Thoughts about how Congress changed the future forever with the passage of this Act? Before it was changed vs After it’s passing? The history of not just music, but social “norms” that define our beliefs and our biases, even today. The early record companies such as Victory, Columbia, both incorporated in the 1880’s-1890’s before sound was considered a “work.” A copyright was given to written “works.” Before player pianos. Musicians we’re called “minstrels.” Music was categorized by the type of live performance. Genre was created for accounting, marketing, manufacturing and distribution. This led to the revision of copyright law. Now, if you did not happen to fit the model defined by the record company, you experienced disadvantage. Did fit the stereotype? “Sorry, not interested.” Now that is the only measure most music consumers apply. Spotify does it. Columbia (now owned by Sony) does it, still! What measure have you been taught for appreciating music, as Art, and are you aware you were taught it?

text: Ever discover new music through a Novel? You could discover a new artist through a song that you just heard on the radio. Or on a Spotify recommendation. You could discover new music through what a friend recommended. Or through a podcast that discusses music. Popularly, you could discover new music by a song that played at the end-credits of a TV show you just watched. Or over a montage scene of a movie. Then - strangely - you could discover new music through a Novel, which is a medium that has no relationship with your ears. (Of course, if you're reading a non-fiction book about music, you could discover new musicians that way.) The first time it had happened to me was with Bret Easton Ellis' iconic "American Psycho". Here is a madman protagonist (in what was obviously a black comedy to me), who had not only killed a guy, but was then harping on aimlessly about the intracies of Phil Collins' output. At the time of reading the novel, I had known Phil Collins' big hits, but didn't know too much about Genesis. It was not too long after reading the novel, I went to my local record store to investigate that band's discographies. Not only did I discover this band because of Patrick Bateman. And not only do I really enjoy Genesis' earlier stuff compared to their later stuff, but I realized why Bateman enjoys the later poppy stuff. The hilarious point of irony was not lost. The last time it happened to me was yesterday whilst reading Pagan Kennedy’s witty "The Exes". I had known many of the acts referenced in the Novel already, except for Mission of Burma, which I've just checked out today, and really enjoyed and have subsequently added to my playlist.

text: Are Janet Jackson’s Control and Rhythm Nation 1814 actually stronger albums than Michael Jackson’s Bad and Dangerous? Michael obviously had the bigger global impact and some of the most iconic singles of all time, but if we judge them strictly as albums , I’m starting to wonder whether Janet’s records are actually stronger. Control feels incredibly focused, with a very clear identity and almost no wasted space. And Rhythm Nation 1814 might be even more impressive: conceptually coherent, socially ambitious, rhythmically innovative, and remarkably consistent from beginning to end. By comparison, Bad has enormous highs, but does it work as cohesively as Rhythm Nation ? And while Dangerous is adventurous and influential, I sometimes feel that it’s more uneven than either of Janet’s albums. So my question is: Would you rank Control and Rhythm Nation 1814 above Bad and Dangerous purely as albums, separate from sales, fame, music videos, and Michael Jackson’s cultural stature? I’d especially be interested in hearing comparisons involving songwriting, production, sequencing, consistency, innovation, and how well each album has aged.

text: Officially A Rock Fan, Somehow After several months of listening to rock, I think I can finally say I’ve genuinely become a fan of the genre. (Reposting this because my previous post got deleted for some reason). What makes this especially strange to me is that I’ve spent pretty much my entire life listening to completely different music. R&B, hip-hop, alternative, soundtracks and plenty of other things, but rock was never really part of my musical world. Going from that to willingly putting on burning riffs, heavy distortion, aggressive drums and music with this much attitude has probably been one of the biggest shifts in my taste ever. There’s something funny about how quickly sounds that once felt abrasive can become addictive. A few months ago, if somebody had told me I’d eventually be putting on hard rock and actually falling asleep to it, I would’ve told them they were full of crap and to move on 😂. Yet somehow my ears have adjusted to all that distortion and weight to the point where it can genuinely feel relaxing now. What has surprised me just as much is how absurdly broad rock actually is. Before getting into it, I mostly thought of “rock” as one general sound. The deeper I’ve gone, the more ridiculous that idea seems. Different decades, scenes and subgenres can sound almost completely unrelated while still somehow belonging under the same enormous umbrella. And despite exploring quite a bit, I keep gravitating overwhelmingly toward classic rock. There’s something incredibly distinctive about it that I haven’t been able to fully put my finger on yet. The guitar tones feel different, the riffs often have more personality to my ears, and the production feels less polished and more real. It’s perfectly imperfect, with a looseness, swagger and attitude that I seem to respond to immediately. What makes that especially interesting to me is that nostalgia can’t really explain it. I didn’t grow up listening to this music. I have no memories attached to these records, no childhood connection to that era and no reason to romanticize it. Yet older rock is consistently what pulls me back the strongest. Modern rock hasn’t connected with me nearly as much so far. Jack White is probably the biggest exception, and one of the few modern artists I fairly consistently enjoy. There’s something in his playing and the rawness of his sound that seems to scratch some of that same itch. So I’m curious about people who came to rock after spending most of their lives listening to entirely different kinds of music. Was the initial transition into all those loud guitars, distortion and aggressive riffs strange for you too? Did your ears gradually change? And for those more familiar with the genre, what do you think actually makes classic rock sound and feel so distinctive compared with most modern rock? Is it primarily production, recording technology, songwriting, guitar technique, cultural context, or something less obvious? And by the way, my favourites so far are Fleetwood Mac and Pink Floyd. I’m also trying to get more into Led Zeppelin but I'm only liking a few tracks. Maybe it'll grow on me later on. And I’m going for more hard rock / Punk. I think i found my way through Chill Rock so now I just need some distorted hard rock music so long as it's not loud for the sake of loudness.

text: Tool, Radiohead, and Arcade Fire (WE) might all be using the Golden Ratio on purpose I’ve been spiraling (pun intended) into this weird theory and now I can’t unsee it: Tool, Radiohead, and Arcade Fire are all using the golden ratio and Fibonacci sequence in their albums—and it seems way too precise to be a coincidence. We already know Tool has been doing this forever. Lateralus follows the Fibonacci sequence in the syllables, time signatures, even the themes. They’re not even hiding it. But here’s where it gets wild: Radiohead’s In Rainbows is 42:43 long. If you go 61.8% in—that’s the golden ratio—you land at about 2:49 into “Reckoner.” That’s exactly when Thom Yorke’s voice lifts, the backing vocals come in, the mood shifts, and you hear the words “In Rainbows” whispered for the first time. Like… c’mon. Now fast forward to Arcade Fire’s WE. That album’s 40:48 long, which puts the golden ratio point at 25:22. And at that exact moment—3:55 into “End of the Empire IV”—Win sings just one word: “I.” Think about that. An album all about “I” vs “WE,” and right at the golden ratio, he says “I.” That has to be deliberate. Also, both In Rainbows and WE were produced by Nigel Godrich, who clearly knows what he’s doing. There’s no way this is accidental. And then there’s the eyeball - Tool’s most recent tour had this huge eyeball visual at the center of the stage—staring straight out at the crowd - WE’s album cover? A massive, all-seeing eye, floating in space. Maybe it’s just a motif. Or maybe it ties into the whole idea of perception, awakening, spirals, the “I” becoming the “eye.” These bands aren’t just writing songs—they’re building experiences that feel aware of you. Like the moment you notice the math… the art is staring back. Anyway, I might be too deep in this, but it’s been tripping me out. Anyone else caught stuff like this in other records?

text: Let's talk about 12 tone serialism 12 tone serialism is a framework for atonal composition created by Arnold Schoenberg in the 1920s, the idea is that instead of using the notes of a given major or minor scale and assigning functions to each of them and their chords (i.e. common practice tonality, the musical understanding that has informed composition from Bach to Beethoven to the Beatles to Beyoncé), all 12 semitones of the chromatic scale are treated equally. The way that serialist music is composed is pretty straightforward, it starts with a tone row, the composer chooses to arrange the 12 semitones in whatever order they'd like, and has to stick with that throughout the piece, he can invert it, put in retrograde, make retrograde inversions (i.e put the tone row backward, upside down, and backwards and upside down) and can of course transpose it, notes from the row can be played in unison like chords, and single notes can be repeated but once you move onto the next note in the row you have to complete the row before coming back it. The 12 tone technique is controversial, its criticized as being robotic or reducing music to algorithms, and many classical music fans think that it's soulless noise. Personally, my favorite atonal work is Schoenberg's pre-serialism "free atonal" Pierrot Lunaire (which is one of my top 5 pieces of music to listen to, and my favorite to play on my clarinet), but I think that 12 tone serialist music can be incredibly beautiful and musical if the composer has good taste, and awful noise if he doesn't, just like tonal or modal music. I especially enjoy the works by the second Viennese school (that is, Schoenberg himself and his students Anton von Webern and Alban Berg) and Igor Stravinsky's forays into serialism toward the end of his life. Here are some 12 tone serialist pieces that you should listen to: Five Pieces for Piano — Arnold Schoenberg (this is the first serialist composition that Schoenberg wrote) Concerto for 9 Instruments — Anton von Webern Threni — Igor Stravinsky (a 12-tone serialist setting to Latin readings from the Book of Lamentations, my church choir and orchestra performed this last year on my insistence and it's such a powerful piece of music) Piano Concerto — Arnold Schoenberg Wozzeck — Alban Berg (Wozzeck was the first serialist opera and it's out of this world, so incredibly powerful) And if you're interested in hearing 12 tone serialist music from other genres, there is a nice amount of serialist jazz as well. John O'Gallagher's interpretations of Webern are a good place to start

text: What are your views on song structure and what music has interesting ones? Intro I rarely see this being discussed but I always found music with a unusual song structure fun to listen to. A lot of modern music it often seems like "verse chorus verse chorus bridge chorus". In some cases there is a pre-chorus before the chorus which although much more interesting, is still overdone. The song doesn't even have to be progressive to have a interesting song structure in my opinion, all genres could use something like this. Here is an example of a Melodic Death Metal song that I think has really cool structure. Melodic Death Metal is usually known to be catchy rather than inaccessible. [Terminus by Dark tranquility] (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jcJfCZQJuHk) Song Structure: C1*R1C1* V1V2V1 R1C1 V1V2V3 R1C1 B1B2S1V1* V2V1 R1C1 Explanation of the notation I used So I wrote it out with my made up notation to make it shorter. I'll explain what I mean. A letter-number combination is essentially one melody section of the song, with the letter denoting section and the number denoting number. For example, C1 would mean chorus melody 1. V1 would be verse melody 1, and V2 would be verse melody 2. R, B, and S stand for riff, bridge, and solo respectively. A letter-number combo followed by a star would mean the verse is modified. In this scenario I mean it is the same melody but without lyrics. The specific song So, now onto the song. I think it is cool because it's like a small and a big sandwich. The first verse has V2 (meat) sandwiched in V1 (bread). The section in the video linked that corresponds to V1V2V1 is 0:47 to 1:13. The rest of the song is an even bigger sandwich with V1 as the bread. If you don't see this I mean the whole section V1V2V3 R1C1 B1B2S1V1* V2V1 which is 1:40 to 3:49. So far, I have only heard one song with a "sandwich structure" even though it seems like it could be common. The structure really makes the song sound much better. Imagine the exact same song instead with the structure V1C1V1C1S1C1, which the basic structure I talked about at the start. The song would still be good, but it just doesn't sound as cool. Another structure I really like There is another structure that I have heard in several songs that I love yet is still not widely used. A simple form of this structure would be V1C1V2C1C2B1C1C2. Basically, at the end of the first verse there is a chorus, but for the second verse and bridge, there is an additional chorus that is completely different. An example would be Kirisute Gomen by Trivium. Even if you don't like the song, you got to admit that that structure makes it sound interesting. Conclusion In my opinion, changing the song structure is a way to make music sound interesting without making it odd sounding or inaccessible. And I mean changing the structure in a way where there is still repetition, so something that is literally melody 1, melody 2, melody 3, melody 4 doesn't fit the bill, because that is essentially just 4 different songs. What do you think about song structure and what are some songs or artists that have really cool structures?

text: [List] What are the most important musical techniques/building blocks to be introduced *after* 1960? I'm using a narrow definition here: -Compositional techniques, not combinations thereof. For instance, hip hop (the genre) didn't appear until the 1970s but its basic building blocks (deejaying/record manipulation and rapped vocals) are both older - with the latter arguably going back to slavery times. Ed note: However, compositional techniques include things like time signature changes (beloved during the 1950s by Moondog) -In order to "count", it cannot have been commercially recorded before 1 January 1960. -It has to be audibly different from anything that a listener would've experienced on 1/1/1960. Synthesizers do not automatically count as they often sound indistinguishable from early electronic music made with oscillators, organs, and tape manipulation - even if it's a helluva lot more efficient to record trance music with a synth and DAW as opposed to recording it piece-by-piece, Tom Dissevelt-style. A lot of modern electronic music techniques - as well as guitar effects pedals - are simply more efficient interfaces to achieve what would previously require a lot of manual amp/organ manipulation in 1959. Here are the largest truly novel (and audibly novel to a listener from 1959/1960) music building blocks I can think of that were first recorded after 1960 off the top of my head: -Auto-Tune. Although vocal manipulation is much older, Auto-Tune relies on software that was not invented until the 1990s. The closest pre-1960 analogue to it might be either the chipmunk effect or some old Alvino Rey records that use a sort of talk box. -Slap bass, the sound used in the Seinfeld theme. Invented in the 1970s by some guy named Larry Graham. Slap double bass, though, dates back to jazz. -Beatboxing. Although there are also older parallels (eefing, some old blues songs), beatboxing is intended to sound like a drum machine and is first documented in the 1960s. -Record scratching. Invented in the 1970s by Grand Wizzard Theodore. I'm completely open to corrections and additions so feel free to add them.

text: Is there an asymmetry to how music critics discuss “simple” and “complex” music? Technical virtuosity and emotional expression are often considered mutually exclusive ideas. I disagree. I would actually posit that prog, jazz, metal, or otherwise maximalist musicians are actually deeply passionate about what they do, often have something unique and profound to say, and are choosing to express themselves with a more advanced form of language, much like poets or playwrights. And rather than attacking the language outright, we should grant these musicians the same grace we extend to three-chord singer-songwriters and ambient synthesists, who are often considered more “honest” artists.  What critics call “bloat” can actually serve distinct artistic purposes: Long-form composition can signify a vast journey, literally or metaphorically, and allow the writers ample time for motivic development. Shifting key centers or time signatures can indicate changes in mood or atmosphere. Use of atypical or mixed modes can communicate an unusual or “outsider” perspective. Maximalist arranging can take already large emotions and make them overwhelming. Exceeding the established limitations of musical convention can communicate a deep spiritual transcendence.  And yet, often when an artist shows a level of ambition beyond what is “cool,” they are often hit with lazy shorthand words like “overwrought,” “self-indulgent,” or the worst offender “masturbatory.” Conversely, minimalism is granted profundity by default. Restraint is always seen as a sign of “maturity.” Records with a lot of emptier space leave a considerable amount of room for the listener to project their own feelings, increasing a sense of depth that may or may not already be there.  This leads to a broader follow-up question: Should paid professional music critics have a better understanding of concepts like composition, arranging, and musicianship? Consider the absurdity of an NFL sportswriter who doesn't know the basic rules and regulations of football; or a food critic who couldn’t distinguish between common cooking methods or ingredients. Why do we allow music critics to feel everything out on vibes instead of insisting that they show a firm understanding about the building blocks of their chosen medium?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Let's talk: What is good songwriting? This topic came to me when I was watching The Needle Drop's review of the new Ghost album. He mentioned how the band separates itself from other metal bands by having tunefulness and good songwriting. I understand that this could vary by genre, and what the artists intent really is. I'm just wondering what makes a song have good or bad songwriting. I've been listening to songs that I enjoy, and songs that I don't care much for to try to understand the differences. So I'm hoping you guys can give examples of good and bad. I don't think this question is completely broad, but it might be subjective. A few questions that come to mind. 1. What makes a song have good songwriting? When I hear something like Future People By Alabama Shakes I think of something that has good songwriting. The song seams to transition extremely well between each of the sections. The note choices, nothing sounds hokey. After the first chorus they introduce a guitar riff for a few measures, then quickly transitions back to the verses. Small subtle nuances to keep the verses interesting. Then after the second chorus it expands on that guitar riff after that first chorus. It's not the pinnacle of great songwriting, but it's something that i've been recently listening to that jumps at me for having good songwriting. 2. What makes a song have bad songwriting? Bad Blood By Taylor Swift. While the song appears to be a remake from the album version, but the song doesn't build off of each other. The verses with Kendrick sounds like a different song, and sound kind of tacked on. The song follows that predictable format of having the beat switch and get rhythmically faster until the ultra simplistic chorus comes in. Then back to the transition to the rap verses which don't make any sense. The song goes into the mellow part at the end, which had no connection to what previously was introduced, then the rhythm speeds up until you go back into the chorus. It just makes me think of really lazy songwriting. I'm not saying that songs that have different sections are bad. Paranoid Android from Radiohead, Day In The Life by The Beatles, and many Progressive Rock songs segue into multiple parts. It's just how it's presented. 3. When is bad songwriting ok? I think when an artist has an intent outside of the pop realm of songwriting, you can transition away from "traditionally" good songwriting like Franky Teardrop by Suidide. A song like this does not have the same intent that traditionally a pop song would. It's experimental by choice. It's not trying to have wide spread appeal, it's pushing the sonic boundaries. Avant-garde if you will. Let me know what you guys think!
label: Deep Analysis

text: Bossanova: the Pixies gone beautiful The combination of abrasive noise against pop song structure is the backbone of most great punk. The Pixies weren't punks, but they utilised that same formula within their alternative rock sound: "Gigantic", "Debaser" and "Where is My Mind" are great examples of how to push volume whilst keeping the listener hooked to the music. Their lyrics also reflect this attitude: weird, kooky, violent, but funny and clever enough to keep the listener engaged. Surfa Rosa, though not really to my tastes, foreshadowed the next decade of rock music. Doolittle is a masterpiece whose praises I don't need to sing: 15 vignettes ranging from the exhilarating ("Slicing up eyeballs!), to the cutesie ("All I'm saying, pretty baby/ La la love you, don't mean maybe") to the hilarious ("Crack-crack-crackity Jones!"). Their fourth album, Trompe Le Monde, is pure noise and fun- not as seminal as the first two, but hardly a disappointment. And Bossanova- well, Bossanova is the weird one, incongruous with the rest of the discography. It's not like the Pixies stopped fishing for noise and hooks: "Rock Music" and "Hang Wire" are as loud and catchy as anything they ever recorded. What's weird is that, for once, The Pixies are po faced. They're not trying to make us laugh; nor are they trying to juxtapose volume against lightness. They're trying to make something beautiful. The love songs on Doolittle were goofs: "La La Love You" was a silly little sketch; "Here Comes Your Man" had tongue firmly in cheek. By comparison, Bossanova's "Velouria" and "Ana" are hungry and euphoric. Had "The Happening" been on any other Pixies album, it would have been a joke. Here, however, Black Francis makes driving into Area 51 to meet aliens sound like he's touching the face of God. "Havalina", the album's finale, is beautiful in a very special way. One small moment, " Walking in the breeze/ On the plains of old Sedona, Arizona/ Among the trees", becomes an ode to the brightness of life and existence. Joey Santiago (AKA the world's most underrated guitarist) gets on board right away, producing as many gorgeous riffs as he does loud ones. But one of the most important musical changes to band on this album is Black Francis' voice. It's still got dynamite, but now it also seems richer and with a wider range. I would bet any amount of money that he got some singing lessons in preparation for this album: the vocal prowess he shows on "Havalina", "The Happening" and "Stormy Weather" is unlike anything on their first two albums. Perhaps I prefer the explosiveness he showed on Doolittle. But the beauty his voice shows here certainly gives it a run for its money. So yeah, I love this album. Not as much as Doolittle, but it's probably my second favourite Pixies LP. Beauty and noise are a hell of a hard combo to pull off, but the Pixies do it with gusto. Anyone else got love for Bossanova? How do you think it compares to the Pixies' other albums? Penny for your thoughts?
label: Deep Analysis

text: What music, genres and styles of music production do you see picking up and becoming increasingly popular? Here’s mine: Hyperclub: it seems techno kick drums and some of the elements of techno, trance and hardstyle production somehow managed to sneak into the mainstream. Lots of artists that you wouldn’t necessarily label as techno or trance currently use a lot of music production elements from those genres. Probably best example is Charlie XCX, but there’s a ton of others as well Oklou-type music: it’s hard to put this one into a specific category but there’s a lot of music being made that has a sort of hushed, ethereal sound combined with trance pads and r&b vocals. Other examples from popular music include Addison Rae. 2000s pop inspired music: Best example is Pink Pantheress. There’s a revival of the sound that was popular in early 2000s pop, and it’s making its way into the mainstream. Hardcore punk revival: the genre is having a bit of a moment and getting a bit of traction that it didn’t have a few years ago. Bands like Turnstile, Knocked Loose, maybe even High Vis are on their way up (well, Turnstile is already there), and so is hardcore. I wouldn’t be surprised if we start seeing hardcore elements more often in mainstream music, specifically in grime, hip-hop and trap. Bob Vylan is a good example. Modern jazz: the London jazz scene is massive and growing. While elemente of jazz have been on their way up for quite a few years (Mac Miller’s production on the last album is an example) I wouldn’t be surprised if more and more people go to see jazz bands, that are increasingly genre-blending and fun. I’d go as far as to give Kali Uchis as an example of someone from the mainstream that has been adopting bits of jazz-inspired instrumentation for years. Rise of reggaeton: already super popular, but paradoxically it seems to be growing in popularity 90s rock and nu metal: not really having a revival, but there’s more elements of nu metal and 90s alt-metal being used by bands. Spiritbox and Wargasm are in this category. While a modest trend now, I wouldn’t be surprised if in 2-3 years there’s a full revival Slacker indie rock and alt-folk: it’s always been there and it never went away, but it seems to be the dominating sound at the moment in indie rock. MJ Lenderman, Alex G’s latest album, Big Thief.
label: Deep Analysis

text: [List] Broadly speaking, how many major categories and approaches to music would you say there are? I'm not asking for every single genre and subgenre that ever existed. I don't think that will ever stop. But I was wondering: are there broad ways we could try categorizing approaches to music? For instance, I've been trying to find ways to generally summarize. Some categories end up overlapping because of multiple traits: Back-to-basics (certain varieties of punk, roots music) Avoiding tonality and conventional musical structure (noise music, ambient) Using different instruments (guitar, synthesizers) Influence from the art world (art music, progressive music) Playing something live versus piecing things together in studio Improvisation vs following a score or planning something out I understand that this topic will likely end up with a large amount of categories anyway, especially with all our varying perspectives on music. But I want to at least see if we can narrow something down.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Well over a decade later, Flying Lotus's "Cosmogramma" taught me that perfection within composition lies within imperfection. Back in 2011, I had a personal musical renaissance. After realizing the sheer discovering power of RYM for the first time, I was expanding my taste outside my normal boundaries, searching for more challenging and unconventional artists and albums from what I was already listening to, from all decades and cultures. It was a pivotal point of my life for me that defined how I perceive and identify with music, which influenced the output of inspirations in my own creations. The album that stuck out the most during this time was Flying Lotus's Cosmogramma, an album I undoubtedly hail as a modern masterpiece and an event of the 2010s. Though I'm not primarily an electronic artist myself, the way Steven Ellison composed the album was unlike what I've heard before, and made a part of my brain come online. It taught me that controlled chaos and the importance of projecting any and all ideas you have in your head at any given time lends themselves to unique and interesting songwriting, no matter what genre or style, especially when presented in an album with fascinating concepts and aesthetics that all synergize with each other. My favorite way to visually describe this album is that it's a sonic representation of the paint section in a hardware store after a heavy earthquake. The song flows in a stream of consciousness, without structure but in an order that can be followed without sounding too jarring in transition. I've seen the album considered as electronic, space jazz, and hip-hop, and though it leans heavily toward electronic (IDM, in particular), naming it solely as such wouldn't do its style justice. The genre-fluid nature of Cosmogramma is a byproduct of its brilliance, another aspect, in my opinion, of what makes an album a more pleasurable listening experience, compared to another album that might have the same colors of sound and styles through the songs across the board. The album was mostly produced in the box through Ableton, with the exception of live recorded bass, harp, and various samples, and was recorded primarily off the grid, which is insane for an electronic album edited in a DAW, as textured as it is. Anyone knows that trying to edit in a DAW off the grid is a nightmare, let alone mixing the texturally dense projects, its nearly impossible to have all instruments sit perfectly together in one space of the spectrum, but if the goal was for all instruments and sounds were perfectly "balanced", I honestly think it would have made the end product boring. Harps are played in no particular meter, samples of ping pong balls are made into beats, hi-hats and snare hits are glitched and stuttered at random and not repeated again in any particular structure, underneath staccato'd synth and sample hits. This frantic style of writing and recording ties into the concept of dreaming, drug trips and OOBEs that Ellison was trying to convey, and is spiritually connected to the death of his mother, in which he had sampled sounds of machines from her hospital during the time of producing the album. A work of Cosmogramma's nature would be incredibly difficult to ever replicate, and has yet to be and may never be. In theory, describing the album in words makes it seem like it would be a mess, which it is, but the imperfection of the arrangement over beats and exceptional production is what prevents it from being perceived as a cacophonous. The more color you have in music, the more vivid the imagery, therefore the greater the listening experience. Cosmogramma is an album that you literally hear something new each listen. It's one of the few albums I would consider an opal for its insane and complex sonic iridescence.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Musical lineages [list] 300 years ago, Johann Sebastian Bach wrote a piece which is rarely discussed among his works. Most people focus on the Cello Suites or Toccata and Fugue in D minor but this piece would go on to have a very interesting influence. 45 years ago, Stevie Wonder took the riff from this piece and repurposed it for a song from Songs in the Key of Life, one of the most acclaimed albums of all time. 26 years ago, Coolio sampled this song and changed up its chorus to create his biggest hit and one of the most recognizable rap songs ever. And 25 years ago, Weird Al parodied that song to create perhaps the greatest work out of all four: Amish Paradise. In a world where sampling has become more and more prevalent and where music has always taken influence from other music, what other some other examples where something obscure, underappreciated or unexpected went through a journey of inspiration until it became something radically different?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Can a song still be an "instrumental" if there are some vocal lines in the song? Consider this I got Rhythm version by the YellowJackets. It starts instrumentals-only, but at 3:11, some vocals come in. Would you still count it as an instrumental? My friend says, as long as there's even a single word spoken or sung, it is by definition vocal music. Calling I got Rhythm an instrumental is wrong by definition. If anything, you'd have to say "the song is an instrumental until 3:11 and then vocal elements are introduced", but calling the whole song an instrumental would be wrong. I say, a song is an instrumental as long as the instrumental aspect is more present/prevalent. Even if there are vocals present in I got Rhythm, they play a secondary role, so for me the song is still an instrumental. Who is right?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Why does "It's Your Thing" by The Isley Brothers sound so incredible? This song sounds so yet so incredibly ahead of it's time and very modern and contemporary in terms of it's production and sound. You could drop it into 2026 and it wouldn't sound out of place at all. I've been listening to "It's Your Thing" by The Isley Brothers a lot recently - especially during the commute to work - and my God, I've always loved the song - who doesn't like this song? it's absolutely perfect - but it's only recently I've come to realise how incredible the production and recording of this song is. It sounds so incredibly modern and contemporary. It does not sound rooted in the late-60s/early-70s at all, even compared to other well-produced and recorded songs of that time. If Bruno Mars released this exact same song this year, and I mean just stripping away the vocals and putting his vocals over the existing track and releasing it as a single, it'd be a worldwide smash hit. The song feels so ahead of the curve in how it's produced, mixed, mastered, arranged and recorded. It does not sound dated in the slightest. Maybe I'm exaggerating how modern sounding it is. I dunno, for me, it just sounds so ahead of it's peers. I definitely think it'd fit right in with the pop hits of the early-to-mid-2000s before trap music took over in the late-2010s. I was trying to think why it sounds so incredibly modern and contemporary compared to it's contemporaries - even in genres outside of R&B/soul/funk - and I think I've come up with some reasons. First: the instrumentation itself. It's got a very tight and repetitive groove, a strong, syncopated bassline, and a structure focused more on rhythm rather than melody. It fits in right with a lot of hip hop and modern R&B. There's also no heavy orchestration like other R&B and soul hits of the 60s and 70s. There's no syrupy strings, no over-layered production. It's just drums, bass, guitar, horns and vocals. Circling back to that impeccable groove, the rhythm section is extremely tight. The groove feels almost loop-like, which I think is why it sounds contemporary. Modern music often relies on loops and quantised rhythms, but here it’s humans playing with that same precision and pocket. The rhythm section of this song is absolutely sensational. One of the greatest I've heard. The drummer and bassist lock in with a feel that wouldn’t sound out of place sampled in a 90s hip hop track. The song also sounds clean and punchy. The result is a dry, punchy, percussive, upfront sound. I think honestly that dryness is really key. It's not trying to create space of ambience. Earlier popular records often sound dated because of excessive room ambience or echo. This track avoids that.It’s dry, tight, centered, and controlled. That alone makes my brain register it as modern. It’s also not constantly evolving or adding layers the way older songs often do. It finds a groove and really rides it. For me, that's a very modern mindset, where the hook is the feel itself, not constant musical change. And this is not the only Isley Brothers song that sounds way ahead of it's time. "Shout Pt 1 and 2" I could not believe came out in 1959. From a technical soundpoint, that song sounds far beyond what was happening in that time period. It's got a loud, chaotic vocal, a call-and-response that makes it sound like a live record, and this sense of an absolute controlled mess. Very raw compared to most late-50s pop and R&B which was very polished, smooth, controlled and arranged. The only song I can compare it to really from that period is "What I'd Say" by Ray Charles. I dunno, just wanted to make this post to discuss this song and The Isley Brothers in general. They don't seem to get discussed much online but they made some fantastic and groundbreaking songs and honestly, they made some really good albums too. Particularly by the standards of R&B, funk and soul music of the time. 3 + 3 is one of my favourite albums of 1973 and that's a Top 5 year for me of all time, and The Heat It On is a very good album as well.
label: Deep Analysis

text: What are some bands/albums that use unpopular or unliked techniques to good effect? As a child I always loved What I Am by Eddie Brickell & The New Bohemians and would always get excited when it came on the radio in my parents car. To this day, something about the guitar in that song really gets me. So recently I decided to listen to the album (Shooting Rubberbands at the Stars) and was pretty surprised by a couple things: First, the album is, in my opinion, a fantastic alt-rock album. While the structure of the songs themselves is not innovative, the lyrics are strong, the instrumentation is skilled, and the melodies are interesting. I am surprised that no other songs were able to take off quite like "What I Am." It seems like the album was a bit ahead of it's time too, having been released in 1988 but having some of the hallmarks of the alt-rock that would dominate the next decade, including the very Dave Matthews-like vibes of songs like Beat The Time, 6 years before DMB's first album was released. But more importantly, I was shocked to realize that the album heavily used the (now unpopular) big production styles associated with 80's music... but it a way that was much different than anything I have heard before and did an incredibly good job of it. I think some of the best examples of what I mean are the synths in Circle, the big drum sound in Love Like We Do, and the bass in Now. I think the difference is that, while these unpopular techniques were used, they were used in more subtle or subdued ways than how we typically think of them. Have you ever had an experience like this, where something that you're typically not a fan of is used in a way that you end up enjoying? What about it did you end up liking?
label: Deep Analysis

text: What's your opinion on 3rd verses in pop songs/Why do you think they went away? As a teenager that got into 80's-90's pop, I noticed that most songs had 3rd verses in replacement of a bridge or will have a 3rd verse AND a bridge. However, I noticed around the mid to late 2000's that VCVCBC became the structure used by the vast majority of the pop industry. If the change had came later on (like in the 2010s) I would have probably blamed it on songs being generally shorter. But the tides turned much earlier than that. Were songwriters getting tired of 3rd verses? Was there some big pushback from the public? Why did it (mostly) go away? I'm also interested on what people think about this structure. I think it can either help a song, or make it overstay it's welcome. Prince in particular was great at making 3rd verses work (No surprise there). I do think sometimes it can be a lazy way of incorporating a bridge without having to compose a new section.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Wall of Voodoo's CALL OF THE WEST (1982): So Much More Than "Mexican Radio"! For this week's album review, I am once again diving into the realm of alleged “one hit wonders” who had a lot more going on than just one song. This time, it’s Wall of Voodoo, and their 1982 LP, Call of the West. It’s a shame, if you ask me, but most people who have heard anything at all by Wall of Voodoo know them for what is probably the least interesting song anywhere on this album: “Mexican Radio.” Get caught eating barbecued iguana once, and you never live it down, I suppose. “Mexican Radio” isn’t a terrible song, but I do think it’s the least effective expression of this album’s core themes on offer. As its title implies, Call of the West is a semi-concept album, focused around the mythic image of America and the Far West. It was actually Wall of Voodoo’s second LP--a followup to their 1981 debut, Dark Continent. Despite that title, it isn’t an album about Africa, but rather one that has a lot of thematic common ground with Call of the West: blue-collar angst, disaffected and brutal masculinities, and a whiff of things strange and surreal. Aside from the themes, the basic musical structure of tracks like “Two Minutes Till Lunch” is reminiscent of the style of Call of the West as well: dense, clattering mechanical rhythms, ghoulish flourishes of harmonica, and frontman Stanard Ridgway’s unmistakable, dipthonged speak-singing, seemingly delivered exclusively through the side of his mouth at an odd angle. But Dark Continent is a bit harsher overall, with more of a foothold in the punk side of post-punk. Call of the West is an album in the full flush of New Wave: quirky, tongue-in-cheek, and not afraid to lay down a bit more synthesiser. While “Mexican Radio” reads as almost disposably gimmicky, like a musically competent novelty song, I think the other tracks on the album strike more of a balance between wicked irony and being unironically enjoyable. “Tomorrow” is, by far, the track on this album that I think most deserves to have been its big hit single. Despite its privileged position as opening track, an affable, lightly electronic soundscape, and rather singable pop hookiness, it was actually never released as a single at all! I think “Tomorrow” does a great job at being something very fun, but also something a bit daring and artistic. It’s easy to love a sort of relatable, goofy song about procrastination, but its “apocalyptic” finish turns it into something a bit more profound. I think Call of the West shines even more once we get away from three-minute pop songs and into the album’s more atmospheric tracks. While the heavy use of rhythm machines is a hallmark of the album overall, and stands out given its rarity on such an early and rock-oriented album, “Hands of Love” is probably the composition centered most tightly around the instrument. Aside from that, what I think always brings me back to this track is the vague, shadowy quality of its lyrics--some details are familiar, but the overall picture is hauntingly unnerving. Several tracks on Call of the West present the theme of loneliness and social isolation, toying with the American myths of rugged individualism and the empty expanse of the West. “They Don’t Want Me” tackles outright rejection by others in a direct manner, whereas the narrator of “Tomorrow” ruins their own relationships through fecklessness. “Mexican Radio,” of course, introduces a character so desperate for companionship that they seek it in a language they don’t even understand. But I think “Hands of Love” reigns supreme here, with its motif of hands losing their grip...perhaps losing their grip on reality. Besides the loneliness resulting from the spread-apart American landscape, other tracks on the album address the lifestyles of the down and out--people who have put their faith in an “American Dream” of independence and self-reliance, but failed to achieve prosperity. We meet compulsive gamblers in “Lost Weekend,” a doomed secret agent in “Spy World,” and, on “Factory,” perhaps the album’s most riveting character of all: a factory labourer whose work has disabled him both physically and mentally. Like so many exploited workers in America, the narrator of “Factory” has no class consciousness, and seems unable to imagine a better or different life for himself, or strive for anything more than the banal comforts of consumerism. But he tells of a phantom itch in his missing thumb, which we might interpret as a metaphor for the vague, gnawing idea of other possibilities...particularly as he remarks that as a child, he was told he could be anything he wanted. The arrangement of this track buries Ridgway’s lead vocal to an extent, though never so much that we can’t make out its harrowing lyrics. I imagine it’s a representation of how suppressed the narrator’s internality and sense of self has become. On the cover of Call of the West, we find a mysterious, crooked door, which is just slightly ajar, inviting us into this album’s strange world. It’s the only feature in a desolate red desert-scape, besides the outline of some bluffs against its horizon. It could be the landscape of Mars just as easily as it could the wide-open emptiness of the Far West. Just as the album’s title implies being welcomed or beckoned into the mythic West, the cover art is darkly inviting to the viewer. While I don’t normally discuss the visual identity of albums outside of their front cover, I do want to make an exception for Call of the West, whose liner notes show the interior of the implied dwelling, decorated with a slew of peculiar trinkets: a taxidermied crocodile, a spilling bottle of liquor, a statue of a buffalo, and what appear to be antique slave shackles. There’s a lot of rich symbolism here, and I think it’s a beautiful addition to the album’s themes, but I never saw it until I owned this album on vinyl! In the age of digital music, we often lose some of these more complex touches when “album art” is reduced to a single square image, and that’s quite unfortunate. Despite having a relative breakout hit, Call of the West would prove to be the final album Wall of Voodoo released with their original lineup. Frontman Stanard Ridgway would pursue a solo career, scoring a surprise hit in Germany with his 1986 single “Camouflage,” a ghost story set during the Vietnam War. He’s remained active as an independent artist through the 2010s. The rest of the band kept the name Wall of Voodoo alive for the remainder of the 1980s, replacing Ridgway with Andy Prieboy. My favourite track on Call of the West is its title track, which is the final track on the album. Like a lot of title tracks, it’s lengthy enough that you can really sink your teeth into it, and serves as a sort of summation of everything that’s happening throughout the album. It’s got cowboyish guitars, yipping coyotes, and a striking transition to a spoken-word bridge, which flows naturally from Ridgway’s unmannered vocal style. That’s all I have for today--thanks for listening! DISCUSSION POINTS: What other albums have cover art that gains a lot from pairing with the back of the sleeve, or the liner notes? What’s your favourite would-be hit single that never got a single release? How high is your tolerance for musical quirkiness?
label: Deep Analysis
